#7857. E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A new JAMA study shows e-bike injuries in kids climbing quarter after quarter. Two pediatric physicians break down who’s ready to ride, which bikes and helmets to choose and when a crash means a trip to the ER.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 19, 2026

E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

“It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt says. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

Timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he says. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”

In the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt says, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

A child is ready, Natt says, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

Class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt says, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

Timmons says a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

Keeping it on is another matter. Timmons says fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

After the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt says. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

Any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons says. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

Watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons says. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

If the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons says, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

“These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt says. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”

#7856. Nick Viall Opens Up About Fatherhood

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he currently co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

What viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he says. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

How's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

Overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

For the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

In terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

And so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

So I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

Well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

And it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

But thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

And certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

It's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a big focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

That's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

Well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

And I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some new young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really important to them.

Once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

It's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

#7853. Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

He also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

What Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most important thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

She doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A big part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

She knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

#7851. Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million company without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event

Home / Health & Wellness / Women's Health

Motherly hosted some of the country’s most influential women leaders for a State of Motherhood event that took a deep look at what the last decade reveals about moms, and what we need going forward.

By Audrey Goodson Kingo Updated Nov. 19, 2026

Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

The conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms said motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

“The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” said Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”

Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie, IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition company Once Upon a Farm.

Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

“Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she said. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

That’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified company offering organic refrigerated baby food, she said. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

It’s all baked in, pun intended, to the company’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner says. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner said, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”

When it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”

Finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner said. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”

Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

“We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she said. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”

Next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

“I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”

Lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, said she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”

“I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani said. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”

It’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, said Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to big tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”

Michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, said she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s new podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”

She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

When it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, said Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology company Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

“I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is important]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”

When it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” said Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”

The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

Guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” said Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”

And bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her new release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, big or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”

That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

“Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of new vertical video shows that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”

#7850. 9 Frozen Puff Pastry Desserts That Only Look High Effort

These treats bring the bakery-worthy wow factor without the professional-level effort.

There are few kitchen shortcuts I love more than keeping a box of puff pastry in the freezer. It’s the secret weapon behind so many desserts that look like they came from a fancy bakery, even when you barely had to lift a finger to make them. We’re talking flaky layers, pretty little twists, golden-brown pastries and impressive-looking tarts, all without the hassle of cutting cold butter into flour while simultaneously pouring in ice water (IYKYK).

If Nutella is your love language, these Nutella puff pastries from A Sweet Thyme need to be on your baking list. Store-bought puff pastry gets brushed with melted butter, spread with Nutella, and sprinkled with ground hazelnuts before being folded, sliced, and twisted into pretty little pastries. They bake up golden and flaky in just 12 to 15 minutes, making them look like something you’d pick up at a European bakery.

You don’t need a deep fryer or a trip to your favorite churro stand to get that cinnamon-sugar goodness. Princess Pinky Girl’s churro twists use just three ingredients — puff pastry, melted butter, and cinnamon sugar — to bring this dream dessert to the table. The whole recipe takes about 15 minutes, which means you can have a batch ready before your guests even finish their first cup of coffee.

If you’re looking for a dessert that doubles as a centerpiece, this strawberry puff pastry snowflake from Sugarbird Cakery & Floral is a showstopper. Despite its impressive appearance, it only requires three sheets of puff pastry, strawberry jam, melted butter, cinnamon sugar, and an egg wash. The finished snowflake is almost too pretty to eat. Almost.

These cherry and cream cheese turnovers from Averie Cooks have serious bakery case energy, but they’re surprisingly simple to make at home. Flaky puff pastry is cut into squares and filled with cream cheese and cherry preserves before being folded into little triangles, brushed with egg wash, and sprinkled with coarse sugar. Don’t skip the best part: a sweet vanilla cream cheese glaze drizzled over the top.

Cinnamon rolls are always a good idea, but making them from scratch can turn into an all-morning project. Barefoot in the Pines’ puff pastry cinnamon rolls give you all the buttery, cinnamon-sugary goodness without the yeast, rising, waiting, and margin for error. They’re especially good for holiday mornings when you want something homemade without adding another complicated recipe to your to-do list.

This caramelized pear tart from Brown Eyed Baker looks like something you’d order at a fancy restaurant, but the secret is just a sheet of store-bought puff pastry. Pear slices are mixed with a homemade caramel sauce in a skillet, topped with puff pastry and baked until golden. Once it’s finished, you flip the tart over to reveal the beautifully caramelized pears underneath. Don’t forget a scoop of vanilla ice cream for serving!

If you love a classic apple dessert but don’t want to fuss with homemade pie crust, consider Well Plated’s upside-down apple tart. Apple slices are arranged over butter, honey, brown sugar, and cinnamon, then covered with a sheet of puff pastry and baked until everything is golden and bubbling. Once you flip it over, the apples are beautifully arranged on top, creating a beautiful tart that looks far more complicated than it actually is — and no one has to know it took just a few minutes to prep.

These cream cheese Danishes from Princess Pinky Girl use puff pastry to create a flaky base for a sweet filling made with cream cheese, maple syrup, yogurt, vanilla, and a touch of lemon juice. They’re perfect for a holiday brunch, dessert table, or anytime you want something that looks like it came straight from a professional bakery.

It seems with the help of a frozen puff pastry, even those of us with nothing left to give can whip up an impressive dessert in no time.

As I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

Don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

However, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

Tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

Don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

In these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

If your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

Would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces new growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

In spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

You’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

This means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7847. The Best Waterproof Gloves of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Nov 21, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Like a rain jacket for your hands, waterproof gloves are essential gear for those working—or playing—outdoors in cold or inclement weather. For outdoor sports enthusiasts, they keep hands dry and protect against frostbite. For those who work outdoors, they are essential because they offer protection from grease, mud, and other wet messes.

We searched out a diverse collection of waterproof gloves for a wide variety of tasks in all seasons. Then we tested their ability to keep hands dry and comfortable in tough conditions. The Carhartt Waterproof Insulated Gloves earned our pick as the best waterproof gloves for men for their reliable waterproofing, comfortable insulation, and affordable price, and the MCTi Ski Gloves for Women topped our women’s picks for their watertight protection, flexible fit, and responsive touch-screen fingertips.

Bottom line: Discover the best waterproof gloves of 2026, tested for durability, comfort, and specific needs, ensuring dry and warm hands in any condition.

We initially selected the following gloves based on the quality of their construction, their durability, and the other features outlined previously. Then we tested them to discover how they held up under wet, slippery conditions. Find out how they performed in the reviews ahead.

Men looking for a long-lasting pair of gloves to keep their hands dry and warm may find what they’re looking for in Carhartt’s waterproof insulated gloves. From the shell to the liner to the palm pad, these gloves are made of 100 percent polyester. They provide a warm, durable, and waterproof barrier between the skin and the elements.

A liner made with Carhartt’s FastDry moisture-wicking technology prevents sweat from collecting inside the gloves, and a waterproof insert provides an extra layer of protection from the elements. Adjustable hook-and-loop closures and elastic cuffs keep hands snug while keeping out cold air and elements.

In our tests, these Carhartt waterproof work gloves were as comfortable as they were waterproof. They performed perfectly on all three of our waterproof tests. They stayed dry under the shower and when immersed in water while providing excellent holding ability thanks to the textured grip area. Three-dimensional construction lets the hand rest in a natural position and delivers good dexterity for gripping and holding. Although we didn’t test specifically for winter warmth, these gloves are deeply insulated for cold-weather work. However, the bulky profile takes away the ability to pick up small or thin items from a flat surface or to reach into a pants pocket.

What our tester says: “These got ‘Best Overall’ because they’re not only toasty and affordable, but they also make an excellent choice for winter chores while not looking like work gloves.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Carhartt waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Women on the hunt for warm, waterproof gloves may want to look at MCTi’s ski gloves. They pair a polyurethane outer shell with a faux leather palm and thumb-grip area for holding ski poles or other slippery objects. On the gloves’ interior, a waterproof liner helps keep moisture from reaching the skin.

MCTi’s gloves also contain 120 grams of Thinsulate insulation that keeps hands warm in temperatures as cold as -10 degrees Fahrenheit without adding much bulk. Handy elastic wrist leashes make keeping track of the gloves easier if the wearer removes them, and sensitive touch-screen pads on three fingers allow the wearer to answer a phone or send a text without having to take off the gloves.

In our tests, these ski gloves by MCTi seemed more like general-use winter gloves. The waterproof feature is on point, with zero water intrusion during testing and a capable grip in wet conditions. Not only that, but the insulation was less puffy than some of the other gloves we tested, which improved dexterity and flexibility for gripping and handling small items. The touch-screen fingertips worked well. Moreover, they’re available in an assortment of accent colors: gray, red, white, rose, and yellow.

Get the MCTi waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Men looking for lightweight protection from the weather may want to consider Ozero’s men’s thermal gloves, which provide warmth and weather resistance without a lot of bulk. These gloves feature a water-resistant and windproof polyester construction that keeps the wearer’s hands dry and warm in inclement weather (most of the shell fabric is indeed waterproof, but the seams and touch-screen pads on two fingers are not, hence the “water-resistant” designation). This pair is a good choice for cycling, running, walking, or other outdoor pursuits.

These gloves may not be well suited to subzero temperatures, but they’re suitable for regular winter wear and have some nice features. The gloves’ thumbs and index fingers contain sensors that are touch-screen compatible, and the palms are covered in grippy silica gel pods to help users maintain a good grip on phones and other belongings. Elastic cuffs keep out the elements. These gloves fit snugly; the manufacturer suggests sizing up for a more relaxed fit.

These mid-weight lifestyle gloves are built for everyday travel and tasks in frosty weather, but not in pouring rain. Our rain simulation and immersion tests revealed numerous water entry points. Water resistance was good in our aggressive rain simulation for about a minute before leaks developed, so we believe the gloves could keep hands mostly or completely dry during an average rainstorm. They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop. Also note that these gloves cost less than most of the others we tested. Moreover, they are slim and flexible and easily fit into jacket pockets.

Get the Ozero waterproof gloves at Amazon or Walmart.

Leather work gloves are a necessity when working near hot surfaces and sparks in addition to protecting the hands from abrasion, cuts, and punctures. Youngstown Glove Company’s FR Waterproof Leather Utility gloves incorporate both leather and Kevlar, a synthetic fabric commonly used for protection, along with a waterproof, windproof, breathable polyurethane barrier. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. However, they don’t provide adequate protection for electrical work.

Youngstown’s waterproof utility work gloves delivered good waterproof and wet-grip performances in our three wet tests. Although we got the leather so thoroughly wet that the gloves became heavy, the waterproof barrier prevented water intrusion to the skin. Wet grip was not a problem. We were pleasantly surprised by the dexterity that these bulky gloves provided, thanks to their three-dimensional construction and a naturally relaxed hand posture. Overall, we would not recommend these gloves for extended use in a watery environment because those conditions would cause the leather to degrade quickly. However, those who need a sturdy and comfortable insulated glove for working in the elements may want to look at these.

Get the Youngstown waterproof gloves at Amazon, JB Tools, or Youngstown Glove Company.

Carhartt’s Cold Snap insulated work gloves offer both cold-weather protection and long-lasting construction that’s tough enough for the jobsite. With warm insulation on the outer shell and a reinforced palm, these polyester gloves are reinforced with leather for extra durability. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment. They have a thick cuff with an adjustable drawstring for improved weather protection. A small section of goatskin around the finger and thumb area provides added grip.

Our second pair of Carhartt waterproof work gloves performed nearly as well as the first. It provided excellent waterproof and wet-grip performance along with excellent dexterity, considering the lofty insulation. The polyester and leather exterior sheds water very well instead of becoming saturated and heavy. We liked the drawcord cuff on these gloves a little less than we liked the hook-and-loop strap closure on our “Best Overall” selection because the barrel-cord tightener is harder to manipulate with gloved hands. Nevertheless, pairing outstanding waterproofing, warmth, and comfort with a great look is the winning recipe for an all-around great pair of gloves.

Get the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves on Amazon.

No more freezing hands when you try to take a pic or return an important text. These low-profile knitted Sealskinz gloves offer triple-layer insulated waterproof, windproof protection from the elements with touch-screen-capable fingertips and outstanding range of motion. The nylon and elastane outer layer offers excellent durability with silicone-printed grips on the palm and fingers for a secure grip. A mid-layer windproof, waterproof, breathable membrane keeps the warmth in and the elements out. The lining is made of merino wool, nylon, and elastane for added warmth and breathability.

These Sealskinz gloves offered a lot of things we really liked but a few things we didn’t. We appreciated that they were truly 100 percent waterproof, both in our simulated rain test and when immersed in water. They also offer outstanding wet-grip capability, with touch-perfect touch-screen functionality. The low-profile design, moderate amount of insulation, and superior wet performance are perfect for getting outside on those miserable raw days when it’s 30 degrees Fahrenheit with freezing rain. But we didn’t love the semi-absorbent exterior because it holds on to more than its share of water, even though the water never reached our hands. It makes these otherwise excellent gloves feel heavy and a little bit squelchy. However, these may be the best gloves when wet weather threatens.

Get the Sealskinz waterproof gloves at Amazon or Sealskinz.

Hestra’s Army Leather Heli Ski 3-Finger Gloves are designed for men and women who spend their time atop some of the coldest mountains. These three-finger gloves are constructed from Hestra’s windproof, breathable, and water-resistant Triton fabric, with goat leather on the palms and fingers for improved grip in cold and slippery conditions.

The insides of these Hestra gloves are made of a very thin polyester fiber with efficient insulating properties, which makes them warm without being overly bulky. The oversize cuffs feature a drawstring closure to keep out snow and moisture, and leashes ensure the gloves won’t get lost. These Army Leather Heli gloves are available in three colors.

These gloves looked great and performed better than expected in our tests, but they were not totally waterproof. We anticipated soaking-wet hands because of the leather and “water- resistant” fabric. In our tests, the leather eventually became wet, and some moisture from outside did seep inside. They offered an OK but not great grip when wet. The best advantages of these gloves are the finger configuration, which offers better warmth than a conventional glove and better articulation than a mitten. That said, we did not test for performance in cold weather. On the downside, the leather must be regularly oiled (a tube is included), and they take a long time to dry once wet.

Get the Hestra Heli waterproof gloves at Amazon, REI, or Backcountry.com.

Built in the style of traditional cuff-length work gloves, Hestra Job Titan Flex Gloves bring the outstanding comfort and durability of goatskin leather with waterproof neoprene cuffs and Hestra Flex fabric. The stress points on the palm and fingers are reinforced with double-layered leather, while the index fingers and thumbs feature touch-screen pads for convenience. These three-season work gloves are lined with moisture-wicking fleece for added warmth and comfort in cold, wet weather.

In our tests, these gloves provided good waterproof protection and excellent wet-gripping ability. They resisted water penetration for over a minute before moisture found its entry point at the edges of the touch-screen pad on the index finger. The touch-screen pad functioned well, and the glove offered good dexterity and comfort overall, but the sizing runs a bit small. The moderate price point and durable construction make them ideal spring, fall, or mild winter weather general-use work gloves.

Get the Hestra Titan waterproof gloves at Amazon.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

#7845. 75 Bougie Gifts That Are So Cool & So Cheap On Amazon

Expensive taste and limited funds? You’ve come to the right place. Amazon is packed with affordable presents that are chic, clever, and impressive, so no one will suspect that you stuck to a strict budget. Best of all, these bougie gifts are so cool, so cheap, and cater to all kinds of interests, so you can cross off your entire shopping list in one fell swoop.

My Bagsmart hanging bag goes with me on every trip because it’s compact while holding all my makeup and toiletries — and I can hang it over doorknobs and towel bars to free up counter space. This hanging makeup bag has a large main interior to hold all of your beauty essentials, plus two fold-out compartments and two expandable side pockets for accessories. Everything zips up into a water-resistant case with a handle for portability.

Shopping for an avid reader? “Got this as a gift and it is the best thing ever,” wrote one reviewer who called this page-turner ring “super cute” and “very convenient.” The wearable remote control hooks around your finger, while the receiver clips onto most e-readers, so you can turn the page from a few feet away and without taking your arm out from underneath the blanket. You can also use it to take selfies from afar.

Plated in 14K gold and covered in sparkly cubic zirconia gemstones, these chunky hoop earrings could pass for the real thing — and you get three pairs for an incredible price. They’re also lightweight and hypoallergenic, with huggie-style clasps for a fit that’s so comfortable, some reviewers sleep and shower with them in.

Yes, they securely grip most types of hair without snagging, slipping, or snapping — but these hair tie bracelets are way more stylish than your average scrunchies. Thanks to their braided designs and metal beads, they look like jewelry when worn on the wrist. Choose from three sizes and dozens of colors and themes.

These grippy socks are made from a breathable cotton-blend fabric with non-slip silicone treads on the bottom for traction, making them a no-brainer for Pilates, yoga, and barre. They also have ribbed ankle cuffs for a secure fit and adjustable ties for style. “Obsessed with these,” one reviewer wrote. “I bought a second pair just to have a few ready for weekly classes!”

These Lego botanical rocking plants are recommended for kids aged nine years and over — but adults love them, too. Each set includes 253 pieces to build two adorable potted plants with smiling faces, colorful interchangeable blooms, and rocking bases. When completed, they double as wobbly fidget toys and nature-inspired decor that doesn’t require any watering.

The most professional person you know probably takes their business cards seriously. This business card holder helps them make a great first impression. Lined with a protective suede texture and made from faux leather in your choice of brown or black, it holds up to 25 cards — and it has a magnetic clasp closure to keep them secure.

Journaling is already one of the healthiest hobbies you can have, but this writing wellness gift set takes mindfulness to the next level. The lined notebook has a 3D finger maze on the cover and textured page borders inside for sensory grounding; the pens have scented aromatherapy ink and bubbly lava barrels for olfactory and visual stimulation; and the highlighters are scented and stackable for immersive fidgeting.

This handwoven bottle strap comes in tons of colors and patterns to suit most personalities. The included silicone strap stretches to fit most popular brands between 12 and 40 ounces, and it has metal clips and strong cotton string for durability.

Gift these three winter beanies to one person so they have plenty of colors to match any outfit, or split them up and use them as affordable yet practical stocking stuffers. Each one is double-layered for warmth and stretchy for a comfortable fit. You can also choose from tons of combination packs that include neutral shades, bold colors, and classic prints.

“There’s not a human that wouldn’t love them” wrote one reviewer who called these plush duck pillows “so cute and squishy.” The fabric is buttery soft, the fiber cotton filling is ideal for cuddling, and the floppy head and feet look adorable propped up on a bed. They’re available in three colors and three sizes — and even the small size is pretty large.

Despite their reasonable price tag, these fuzzy slippers have racked up over 8,000 five-star ratings. They even have an anti-skid rubber outsole, so your giftee can get the mail or take the dog out into the yard.

Travelers don’t have to show up to work trips and destination weddings with their jewelry in a tangled heap. In fact, it’s so compact and convenient that it might just replace their existing storage system: “I love it so much I don’t even use my jewelry box at home anymore,” one reviewer wrote.

Whether their shower is too dark or too bright, this LED overhead lamp gives them fully customizable bathroom lighting. Gift these chic Demitasse cups to the person who adores their espresso machine. A friend gifted me one of these book nook kits for my birthday one year, and assembling it was so fun and relaxing. It now sits on my shelf, where it collects compliments. These reusable hand warmers are a cute, practical gift for the person who’s always cold. Available in seven color options, this strawberry bag charm looks exactly like the real thing. For the jewelry lover who already has plenty of rings and bracelets, this hand chain offers a chic, unique way to accessorize. Since it’s part balm, part lipstick, and part gloss, Clinique Almost Lipstick is my go-to when I want sheer, flushed color alongside shiny hydration. This isn’t your average perfume. According to one reviewer, pin-straight lashes are no problem for this heated eyelash curler: “I use it every day and it’s the only thing I have ever used that actually curls my lashes.” It’s USB-rechargeable with quick-heating silicone pads that change color when they’re ready to go, and you can choose from two temperature settings to lock in curl and volume.

Instead of lightweight fill, this weighted cat plushie contains 1.9 pounds of beads in its belly, providing gentle pressure intended to help regulate the nervous system and offer sensory relief. Give the gift of self-care, even if your loved one only has time for a quick shower. These shower steamers are like bath bombs you can use while standing up. Whether they’re unwinding in the bath, partying in the living room, gaming in their home office, or reading before bed, this crystal light projector helps your loved one set the mood. These oversized sunglasses have thick, rounded frames with UV400 polarized lenses, which make them look and function as if they’re much more expensive than they are. “Well-made sunglasses that look designer without the designer price tag,” raved one reviewer who called them “sturdy” and “comfortable” with “great UV protection.”

This iPhone 14 ripple case is equal parts pretty and practical. Its wavy texture looks stylish while improving grip, and it supports wireless charging, so they won’t have to fuss with removal. Your loved one no longer has to choose between plastic or portability. Hydrating your skin on the go has never been easier — or more satisfying. Since they’re sold in a pack of six different colors, these mini loop stress toys are great stocking stuffers — or you can gift a few and keep some for yourself. Give your favorite skin-care enthusiast a spa-worthy facial without the spa-worthy price tag. According to reviewers, this five-piece makeup set is perfect for people who travel a lot or prefer to streamline their makeup routine. The Running Buddy is a great gift for joggers, hikers, cyclists, gym enthusiasts, travelers, concertgoers, or anyone who likes to travel light. The forgetful friend or the person with pets and kids will appreciate this candle warmer lamp because it provides all the ambiance of a candle without the dangers of an open flame. Buy this purse light for the person who can never seem to find their keys in their giant tote bag. After feeling the impossibly soft texture for myself, these cloud socks have become one of my go-to gifts when I don’t know what to get someone. While it looks like a decorative keychain, this strawberry coin purse doubles as portable, accessible storage for tiny treasures. This isn’t your average water bottle sling. These plug charms adorn most devices while keeping the charging connectors safe from dust, sand, dirt, and water damage. They come in a set of eight charming designs (including flowers, butterflies, bows, and stars), and the plugs fit any device that charges using a USB-C port, including most Kindle e-readers, smartphones, and earbuds.
