#7834. Actress Chloe Bridges and Dr. Charis Chambers on what moms need to know to help protect their baby against RSV infection

In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 25, 2026

This article is sponsored by Pfizer. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

This episode is sponsored by Pfizer. This article is directed to a U.S. audience and may not be suitable for those outside of the U.S. We partnered with them to bring you this conversation, but everything you hear from me, Chloe, and Dr. Chambers is our own experience and opinion. Not medical advice, just a conversation between moms.

Pregnancy has a way of making you feel responsible for someone before you have ever met them. For actress Chloe Bridges and OBGYN Dr. Charis Chambers, that meant navigating the identity shift of new motherhood while also learning about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a highly contagious respiratory virus that is the number one cause of hospitalization for babies in the United States with nearly 50% of RSV hospitalizations occurring during the first 3 months of life. Both moms built a trusted village of support to help navigate – and have a lot to say about what they wish they had known sooner.

In a candid conversation on The Motherly Podcast, Chloe and Dr. Chambers get real about the challenging transition into motherhood, learning to ask for (and accept) help, and what every expecting mom should know about helping protect their newborn from RSV infection.

Chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

Dr. Charis Chambers is a board-certified OBGYN and fellowship-trained pediatric and adolescent gynecologist known to millions online as The Period Doctor. She is the Chief Medical Officer at the cycle-tracking app Clue and the author of The Period and Puberty Parenting Revolution. She lives with her husband, Zachary, and their son, Joshua.

Chloe: I think for me it was that everything is a phase. In the early days, I would get so nervous if something went wrong that day, you know, if he didn’t nap or wasn’t a good sleeper. I’d be like, ‘Oh my gosh, he’s never going to sleep. He’s always going to be a bad sleeper.’ And I just had to learn that a good day today doesn’t necessarily mean a good day tomorrow. A bad day today doesn’t mean a bad day tomorrow. Everything is just constantly changing and in flux.

Dr. Chambers: The first lesson was really that I just can’t do it all by myself. I take pride in being able to accomplish things, and I am so proud of the things I have accomplished, professionally, personally. But motherhood is not one of those things where there’s a badge of honor when you suffer. So I had to learn, from the newborn phase to the late infancy phase to now, that I need help. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. And all of those are really good reasons to ask for help.

Chloe: I didn’t know what I didn’t know. It was almost like I didn’t want to think about postpartum too much, because I truly didn’t know what to expect. Everyone talks about how it’s just such a big transition, and I did really feel that. What’s that thing that people say? Two people are born that day. The baby is born, but then you are also born as a mother. And I absolutely experienced that. You can try to prepare mentally for what it’s going to feel like, but it’s still so surreal when it actually happens.

Dr. Chambers: I immediately threw up my hands in thanks, and then I looked around like, ‘Wait a second.’ Everything is different. I felt like I didn’t even know which way to move or walk. I didn’t know what to do next. I just sat with that moment. My beliefs, my vision for tomorrow, my to-do list, it all just exploded, all in that moment. And it was immense joy, but a nervousness that I think is in proportion to just the depth and caliber of what this is.

Dr. Chambers: As someone who spent so long not being a mother, I never thought that motherhood would ever fully define me, and I still don’t feel that way today. I also think when you desire something so much, it’s hard sometimes to verbalize that desire. So knowing that you’re stepping into this role, this space, that has never really been in your control to step into, but that door is opening. It was an identity shift, but like an identity shift I’d always hoped for but never had the power to change. Becoming a doctor, I knew that. I knew I was going to go to med school. Once I got that MD, I was going to be a doctor. But this is almost like it’s not an earned thing. It is given. I knew it was a forever shift, but spending so much time desiring to be in that role, and seeing that for myself and not knowing if it was going to happen, that was a real identity shift for me.

Chloe: I think a lot of the decisions I was making were just about being so much more cognizant of my own health. Before pregnancy, I don’t know if I was necessarily the healthiest person, but you get pregnant and suddenly it’s not about you, it’s about you and your baby. And your health is intertwined obviously. So it was just a lot of decisions about, you know, obviously I’m going to follow all the advice. I’m going to limit my caffeine intake and I’m going to avoid foods that could give me listeria. And I’m going to, you know, take my prenatal. All of a sudden I was thinking about my health so much more, in a way I hadn’t been before.

Dr. Chambers: So many of the decisions that I knew I had to make, it was almost like I had the answers to the test, just because I’m an OBGYN. But then I started to realize that what I really knew about pregnancy was related to a role that I wasn’t playing this time. I was the actual patient. I had a point in my pregnancy where my cervix was shorter, and they were measuring it, and wondering, are we going to need to do something more invasive, like a cerclage, or can we just do vaginal progesterone. And my very best friend, it was her bachelorette party, but it was in a remote area of Mexico, and I said, ‘How can I reconcile potentially delivering early in this extreme prematurity state that we would be looking at because I just want to be on this girls’ trip?’ I had to just sit with myself, ‘All right, what makes the most sense?’ Of course my friend was amazing and was like, ‘Girl, say less. No one’s going to feel bad. Take care of you and your baby.’ But it just was hard. You want to do so many things, but at the end of the day, you have to stand in your values and stand in your truths and trust that the people around you will be supportive of that.

Dr. Chambers: This day and age, it is just hard, but it depends on the topic. When I was making my registry, for whatever reason, I just couldn’t start it. There’s a billion strollers. What do you mean there’s this many cribs? I was so overwhelmed. So I gave my sister my login and said, ‘Go to town.’ But as it related to my health, being someone who had a high-risk pregnancy, it was a meeting of the minds. I made sure all of my doctors were on the same page, and I wanted a yes. Like when you’re in the emergency row of the flight and they’re like, ‘Yes, yes, yes.’ ‘Nephrologist?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘High-risk doctor?’ ‘Yes.’ OBGYN who’s doing the delivery, yes. I trusted my team.

Chloe: I was also overwhelmed by the whole registry process. But I don’t have a lot of friends who have been pregnant before me, so I was leaning on the internet a lot. Dr. Google, and honestly lots of YouTube videos, all those videos of people being like, ‘This is what’s on my registry,’ or ‘Day in the life.’ And then my OBGYN was so helpful. I would be lost without her. She was truly such a resource, and I really felt like I had built a trust with her, and it really paid off later during birth and everything. I felt like I could ask her anything and trusted her advice.

Dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. This is a very serious thing.

Dr. Chambers: Cold and flu can look like fevers and things of that nature. Sometimes it isn’t terribly respiratory leaning. But RSV has a lot to do with how your baby breathes, the retraction signs, and the work of breathing is the term that we use. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s important to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

Dr. Chambers: During those early months of life, that’s when your baby is at highest risk. Their immune systems are slowly building up, and when we’re thinking about the way RSV might affect an adult, it is not the same for your infant. So if it’s just vaguely on your radar, it’s important to know that this deserves more prioritization. It deserves more energy, more research. If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

To avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

Dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. The RSV vaccination uses that natural process by allowing the mom to create antibodies to RSV and pass them down to her baby. When you get the maternal RSV vaccine, you are helping to protect your baby from the moment they take their first breath. Maternal immunization is an important part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

Chloe: RSV wasn’t on my radar. It was something that I learned about from my OBGYN. She recommended I get ABRYSVO for it, and I remain very happy that I listened to my OBGYN’s recommendation to get ABRYSVO when I was pregnant, and that helped protect him during his first six months of life when he is so vulnerable.

ABRYSVO should not be given to anyone with a history of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any of its components. An increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (severe muscle weakness) was observed after vaccination with ABRYSVO. Please keep reading for full Important Safety Information at the end.

Chloe: I’m glad we’re talking about this, because sometimes it can feel like so many things are being thrown at you when you’re pregnant, especially if you don’t have a lot of knowledge going into it and then you’re hearing about things from your OBGYN. It can feel sort of rushed, where if I’m hearing about a vaccine in my 32-week appointment, but then they’re like, ‘Oh, by the way, you only have until your 36 weeks to get it.’ So the more you know going in, it can only help to be more informed, to have time to do research.

Dr. Chambers: The mental shift that was required the most, that I still carry with myself today, is letting go of the whole independent aspect. I would pride myself in being someone who was very self-sufficient. ‘I got it. If you can’t do this, I’ll figure it out.’ And it’s not that I don’t believe in myself, it is that I fully acknowledge the weight of motherhood and all that is required, and I now welcome the help. I had to tell my older sister, ‘I need you to put together my pump,’ and she did. I had to tell my mother-in-law, ‘The only thing I need today is a nap.’ And she’s like, ‘Go nap.’ Until you learn to verbalize those things and truly believe that you’re worthy of it, not as a point of insufficiency, motherhood requires a village. It requires a team. It requires support. Your mental health will be that much better for it.

Chloe: You go from being an individual with all of your independence, and then suddenly you are putting this baby’s needs before your own. My advice would be to try to establish communication with your village early, whoever that is, and have some sort of plan. Learn how to delegate. I don’t think I had done a lot of delegating before becoming a mom, and then suddenly you’re delegating all the time.

Chloe: I want him to see me as competent and capable, but I also want him to see me as playful and fun. I think that’s been a big part of it. Maybe especially having a little boy, I want to be playful with him, and I want him to be able to have that kind of relationship with me. The nurturing comes so easy, but the playfulness has come a little harder. I hope he looks back and he’s like, ‘You know what? We had fun.’

Dr. Chambers: I hope my son sees me as someone he can trust, as someone who can give him advice, as someone who always makes decisions that are grounded in love and goodness, and someone who’s been making decisions since before he was born to set him up to have the best possible life. I hope that he trusts me with every aspect of who he is, knowing that the love I have is profoundly unconditional, and it has been before I could even picture his face. Before I even knew who he was, he was always worthy of that love and support, and it’s not going anywhere.

This article has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the full episode of The Motherly Podcast on YouTube.

Ask your healthcare provider about the risks and benefits of ABRYSVO. Only a healthcare provider can decide if ABRYSVO is right for you. Always talk to your healthcare provider about any side effects you may experience.

You are encouraged to report side effects of vaccines to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Visit http://www.vaers.hhs.gov or call 1-800-822-7967.

Individuals who received ABRYSVO during pregnancy are encouraged to enroll in a pregnancy exposure registry at 1-800-616-3791. The registry will monitor pregnancy outcomes.

ABRYSVO is a vaccine indicated for pregnant individuals at 32 through 36 weeks gestational age for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and severe LRTD caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants from birth through six months of age.

Please see full Prescribing Information for ABRYSVO at pfi.sr/ABRYSVO_PI.

#7833. Nobody Warned Me About Bladder Leaks Before Becoming a Mom — Here's What I Wish I'd Known

For starters, they’re more common than you’d think.

After having my second baby, my body was a mess: hair falling out, boobs engorged — the works. So when I peed a little when I sneezed, it didn’t seem like a big deal. Until it happened again. And again. Eventually, I managed to sneeze, cough, and laugh without feeling some bladder leakage, but it took a few months for my body to get the memo.

These days, everyone talks about their pelvic floor: what it is, how to strengthen it, how having a baby can wreck it. But bladder leakage — which can be related to that all-important pelvic floor and the stress it undergoes during pregnancy and labor — tends to fly under the radar. No one wants to talk about it, maybe because there’s still a stigma attached to bathroom issues. Even though I’ve discussed every other postpartum thing under the sun (padsicles! Peri bottles! Nipple shields!) with my friends, urinary incontinence has never entered the chat.

But fortunately, Poise is ready to. The brand’s variety of bladder-leakage pads makes it easy to find exactly what you want, be it feels-like-you’re-wearing-nothing protection or a pad that keeps you dry all day. With that, here’s everything I wish someone had warned me about ahead of time.

Bladder leakage might not come up a lot (or at all) in the group chat, but a lot of women experience it. In fact, a large scientific review found that one in three women experiences bladder leakage between six weeks and a year after giving birth — whether it’s their first child or their third. So you’re probably not the only mom at the baby music class who’s dealing with the occasional accident. It only seems like a rarity because no one talks about it, when really it’s a legitimate and very normal part of recovering from birth. And that’s a disservice, because when people aren’t comfortable talking about issues like this, then the solutions don’t receive attention, either.

So you have some accidental leakage and want to give your old period pads a shot. While your average maxi-pad might do the trick if your leak is small, do you really want to risk an impromptu pants change while you’re out and about with your baby? If not, then you might need to consider more protection with a pad that’s actually designed for bladder leaks, like Poise's Pads for Bladder Leaks.

Poise’s pads quickly absorb wetness and trap odor so that no one but you knows what you're dealing with, and they come with layers that wick moisture and keep you feeling dry. On top of up to 12 hours of protection, they stay 25 times drier than the leading period pad. Plus, Poise Bladder Leak Pads have a thoughtful, contoured design that prevents bunching — so you can wear them under leggings and no one will know the difference.

A pad that can handle bladder leakage might sound huge, bulky, and like a wedgie waiting to happen. After all, super-thick pads can get tricky when you’re exercising, might need adjustment when you’re out and about, or can just be flat-out be annoying to wear.

But you don’t actually have to sacrifice comfort for protection. Poise Ultra Thin Pads for Bladder Leaks with Wings can handle moderate bladder leaks, absorbing wetness and neutralizing odors so you feel (and smell) fresh all day. They have layers that have been specifically designed to handle more wetness and help you stay dry, so you can focus on more important things, like enjoying postpartum life!

Bladder leaks after baby make a lot of sense, considering the many ways in which pushing a kid out can affect with your body. But (sorry in advance!) they can also occur at other times in your life, too — like during the menopause transition. It's not that perimenopause itself leads to bladder leakage, but natural changes in your body during this time, such as weight gain and anxiety, can contribute to it, according to one study.

And, as you can imagine when you have a baby bouncing around on top of your bladder (and frequently kicking it), leakage can also happen during pregnancy itself — not just after delivery. It’s actually more common than it is postpartum: Roughly four in 10 women experience bladder leakage during pregnancy, according to one analysis.

This is all to say: Bladder leaks are a normal part of life, whether you’re having a baby, recently gave birth, or are just getting older. And when that happens, it’s a relief to have protection that you can count on — and actually feel confident and comfortable wearing. After all, there are a lot of things to worry about when you become a mom; having to swap out your underwear shouldn’t be one of them.

#7831. What To Buy With Gift Cards: 28 Best Things To Spend Your Holiday Money On

Because nobody else is going to buy you that weighted vest you’ve been eyeballing for months.

And listen, don’t do that thing we all sometimes do and leave them to languish in a desk drawer or a dusty corner of your inbox. January is the perfect time to treat yourself to the stuff you’d never splurge on otherwise. Buy the fancy version of something you use every day! Hit Ulta to refill your empty beauty bottles! Put that Visa gift card toward something that will make you feel better!

Here’s what the Scary Mommy team is spending our holiday gift cards on this year, and we hope you’ll find some inspiration here for your own post-holidays shopping spree.

I love the concept behind this knife: A female chef was tired of all kitchen knives being designed and fitted for men, so she literally took matters into her own hands. Enter the Cardinal knife, which comes with multiple handles for the size of your grip. This is such a great, high-quality knife, and having it fit my hand makes chopping so much easier and more enjoyable. I love the red color, too. And like everything I buy these days, it's dishwasher-safe. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

I love to use holiday gift cards to zhoosh up my normal routine by spending a little more on “everyday” stuff, like fancy toothpaste. Before Oral Care’s whitening toothpaste uses nano-hydroxyapatite, a mineral ingredient that’s having a major moment. Plus, it skips the peroxide, so it’s gentler than the strips that leave my teeth zinging. I also really appreciate that it comes in a recyclable, plant-based tube. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

I feel like I am constantly looking for a flashlight in my house, and when I finally find one, it's out of batteries or not bright enough to help me. This rechargeable flashlight has solved all of my problems. It is incredibly bright, it can either be plugged in or used with traditional batteries, and it is substantial enough to beat an intruder to death with it if it comes to that. I have it in one safe, special place where I know I can grab it quickly when I need it. — Sarah Aswell

If you want to spend a gift card on something you’ll use every single night, a pillow is the way to go, and this one has a curved shape that’s designed to cradle your neck and shoulders whether you sleep on your side or your back. The fill is a copper-infused, CertiPUR-US certified foam that stays cool, plus there’s a hidden zipper so you can add or remove fill until it’s exactly the right height, and it comes with a cooling organic bamboo pillowcase. It’s handmade in California, comes in queen, king, and travel sizes, and has a 60-night trial, so it’s a low-risk splurge. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

I’m spending one of my gift cards on this for my daughter because it’s a screen-free drawing toy that actually teaches her how to draw. The robot scans a card, then uses light and voice guidance to walk kids through each drawing step by step, and it comes with 150 word cards and 12 color pens, so she can learn to draw and read new words at the same time. It’s a Montessori-style, ages 3 to 8 gift that she can use on her own, which means I get a few quiet minutes too! — Katie Garrity

If I’m putting my gift card toward something practical, I want it to be something that still feels like a bit of a splurge. The Shark AquaReach Pro is just the investment. It vacuums and mops at the same time, and the detachable wand lets me clean way past the floor: baseboards, tile walls, under the couch... the whole shebang. This saves me so much time when I’m cleaning the kitchen and bathrooms! — Julie Sprankles

My dad gets me an REI gift card every year — it's a reminder of all the outdoors stuff we did together when I was a kid, which often involved trips to the store (my dad is actually one of REI's earliest members!). This year, I'm going to pick up this Veer Hauler, after years of seeing my friends use similar wagons to haul equipment and luggage on trips. I love this new one because it packs flat, comes with modular packing bins, and can even attach to my bike. I love that you don't have to pack and unpack with this version, and it won't take up the entire back of my car when I bring it places. Cannot wait for this to change my game when car camping this summer. — Sarah Aswell

If you found a Walmart gift card in your stocking this year, I recommend putting it towards this easy home upgrade. The Juliet by SparkPod swaps in for your old shower head in mere minutes, with no tools and no plumber required. It has a two-stage filter designed to cut down on chlorine and buildup without sacrificing water pressure; I genuinely feel like I can already tell a difference in my hair and skin. — Julie Sprankles

If you're deciding where to spend a gift card, put it toward this record membership, which has a real curator behind every pick (Wirecutter even noted the monthly picks are "chosen by humans, not AI"). You build a profile and connect Spotify or Apple Music, and your curator chooses vinyl based on what you actually listen to, with a handwritten note on every record and no duplicates. Plans start at $149, which works out to under $17 a record, and the records are yours to keep, so it's a gift that keeps showing up all year (and a great pick for the hard-to-shop-for music lover)! — Katie Garrity

This has literally become my go-to lip gloss because it has a high-shine finish that manages to not be sticky at all, and it’s super-hydrating thanks to hyaluronic acid, shea butter, and coconut oil. Not to mention, the color Brave (my fave!) is a warm, spicy tint that I swear complements anything. — Julie Sprankles

I have wanted an IPL device for a while, and there's no better time to get one than when you have a gift card burning a hole in your pocket. I chose Ulike because it's highly rated by all the testing sites, and it has a special cooling mechanism that makes hair removal, as far as I can tell, 100% painless. I was a little intimidated at first, but this device is amazing and really easy to use! I hate shaving more than anything, and in just a few weeks, I could see major results from just a few minutes of scheduled use. This is one of those products where I'm surprised not everyone has gotten one. — Sarah Aswell

I live in the coastal South, where it is almost always warm and very humid. So I am a big fan of the idea behind Atmosphera: skincare matched to the climate you actually live in. This Hydra Balance Warm Climate moisturizer is made for exactly the type of weather where I’m from, and I’ve found that the lightweight formula layers so easily under my makeup. Bonus: It helps control shine! — Julie Sprankles

This is a small upgrade that makes brushing less painful: a detangling brush with soft-flex teeth that glides through knots and is designed to minimize breakage and pulling. The tiered teeth detangle and smooth at the same time, so you get a frizz-free finish, and it works on wet or dry hair, including in the shower to spread shampoo and conditioner. It’s made for fine, thinning, or color-treated hair, which makes it a great treat for anyone with delicate strands. — Katie Garrity

I often get at least one beauty gift card, and this year I'll be spending it on this one-and-done moisturizer. As a busy mom I have no time for my tween's seven-step face routine, and if I'm being honest, I'm not going to put on a daily sunscreen unless it is just included in the one thing I slather on my face. I love this product because it feels good going on, especially for how much it has going on. And the packaging is such that it's easy to slip into my bag or travel with it. — Sarah Aswell

Confession: In the past, I have been a chronic nail-biter. Gross, I KNOW. I have always done it absentmindedly when I’m stressed. This is the first product that has ever curbed that inclination. I think it’s because this four-step system air-dries in about five minutes (no UV lamp needed) to a salon-worthy finish that feels a lot like gel nails. They’re so pretty that I don’t want to mess them up! The Cherry Soiree color is my current obsession, although I honestly love all of the colors in the Soiree Collection. — Julie Sprankles

One of the best things to buy with gift cards? Your favorite bras. My new favorite is this lounge bra by Embrace, which is just so soft and comfortable while still supplying enough coverage and support to wear out of the house. I honestly have no idea what material these are made of, but I want my entire wardrobe to consist of it. — Sarah Aswell

I turned 45 and now suddenly I can't see anything!? I fixed it by asking for a gift card to EyeBuyDirect for my birthday this year so I could shop for my own pair of glasses in peace. I landed on this style with round frames and a neat see-through champagne color that I believe makes me look cool instead of old. New glasses are such an easy way to update your style, but I never want other people picking them out for me. — Sarah Aswell

How old am I? I'm so old that I buy laundry detergent with my gift cards. But hear me out! It is so much more fun to wash laundry with higher-end cleaners that work well and smell elevated. — Sarah Aswell

If you’re sitting on a Christmas gift card, this is how I’d spend mine: a lightweight robe made from Cool-jams’ Kottinu fabric that wicks sweat and dries fast, so you can cover up at 3 a.m. or after a shower without heating up. It has a shawl collar, a tie belt, long sleeves, and an easy mid-calf length, and an odor-control finish helps it stay fresh between washes. It’s unisex in sizes XS/S to 3XL and comes with a 30-night trial, so it’s a low-risk treat for anyone who runs hot. — Katie Garrity

These slippers are cozy enough for a slow morning but sturdy enough to wear out for a coffee run, because they’re made with soft nubuck leather and a genuine shearling lining. The footbed is a cushioned, fleece-lined dual-density design that’s removable and washable, and the full-coverage non-marking rubber sole gives you real traction both indoors and out. They fit true to size, they’re $140, and they’re the kind of upgrade that makes you actually look forward to getting home and putting them on. — Katie Garrity

I second everything Katie said about these slippers — this is my go-to brand for flip-flops and slippers because they are high quality and actually get arch support right. No one buys moms slippers anymore at Christmas because it's seen as the first thing anyone thinks of, but it's that way for a reason! No matter, I will take my gift card and pick out my own pair and get exactly what I want. — Sarah Aswell

My gift card plan is to put it toward Nuuly, the clothing rental service where you pick premium brands and try trends without having to commit to owning (or storing) any of it. A gift card goes toward the $98 a month subscription, $22 bonus items, or buying something you love from your rental, and they come in amounts from $25 to $1,500. It’s an easy way to get something new in your closet every month, and it’s an e-gift card, so it’s also great for last-minute gifting. — Katie Garrity

One of my favorite ways to spend holiday gift money is on stuff that centers me. Not anyone else... me. Because really, when else do moms do that? I’ve wanted a weighted vest for so long now, and I really appreciate that the Spy Ruck is designed for women with a slim, contoured fit and padded straps with the weight built right in. — Julie Sprankles

No one is going to buy you workout equipment for the holidays, because that would be a bit insulting. But what if I WANT some workout equipment? I love these new dumbbells from Echelon that double as kettlebells! I have very limited space to work out at home, and I can't have a ton of weights sitting around. These dumbbells help me lift heavier and stay strong while allowing me to vary my workouts a bunch more. — Sarah Aswell

I was over at a friend's house and tried their neck and back massager, and I immediately knew I needed my own as soon as possible. This version hits all the right spots and is heated, too. I can feel the tension leave my back, and it makes me feel relaxed for hours afterward. I've bought them for other people as gifts — and note that it's FSA/HSA eligible! — Sarah Aswell

If strength training is on your New Year’s list like it is mine, a good adjustable bench is such a smart foundation for a home gym. The RitFit Gator adjusts to 21 positions, from flat to incline to decline, so you can do pretty much everything... from chest presses to core work. It’s sturdy, rated for up to 1600 pounds, with thick padding, and it has wheels so you can roll it out of the way when you need to. Did I mention it’s pink?! Such a dopamine boost! It’s a bigger-ticket item, which is precisely why using your gift cards to chip away at the cost is a clever strategy. — Julie Sprankles

If you have a gift card to spend, this is the treat I’d point you to: You lie on thousands of spikes for 20 minutes; the first couple of minutes feel intense, and then it melts into a deep, warm, tension-releasing calm that makes it perfect right before bed. It has an organic cotton cover with a plant-based latex foam fill, and it comes with a free app of guided sessions to help you get through the “ouch” phase. Start with Level 1 if you’re new to it, and know that there’s a 60-day return window if it’s not your thing! — Katie Garrity

Again, gift cards are the perfect excuse to finally buy yourself some of the things you’ve wanted for a while but have put off buying. For me, Spoiled Child is definitely one of them. I’ve been dying to see if it lives up to the hype, and you know, I believe it does! Along with bovine collagen peptides, it has vitamin C and hyaluronic acid, and the brand says it’s designed to support the look of your skin, hair, and nails. It’s nice, too, that the mango flavor makes it easy to just mix it in with your daily smoothie or tea (although I often just shoot it straight!). — Julie Sprankles

We're all thinking it: What better way to spend a holiday gift card than on the newest and most innovative vibrator? Best of all, the brand is widely available, so your distant relative who gave you an Amazon gift card, for example, will never know what became of it. — Sarah Aswell

Ever since we started inviting cats into our homes, humans have been looking for better ways to deal with the unavoidable issue of their waste. Some cats will happily share a litter box, while others will refuse to use soiled litter, even if they are the only cat using it. Inappropriate toileting â that is, peeing or pooping in shoes, on bedding, in fruit bowls(!) â can be a sign of a health problem, but more often than not, itâs about the litter box itself. The wrong location, the wrong type of litter, and most significantly, a box that isnât clean.

The Autoscooper 12 is the newest self-cleaning litter box from PetPivot. The US company was founded in Portland, Oregon, in 2023. Following the overwhelming success of the AutoScooper 11, PetPivot released the new model in 2026, which is available in the US, Europe, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, and Australia.

No more daily scooping. You will occasionally need to give the whole unit a proper clean, but itâs a relatively painless process.

However, the open design provides most cats with plenty of room to move, and with an operating volume of 32 dB, itâs perfect for smaller spaces and apartment living.

But as I discovered, low cost does not mean low quality.

Unlike my other unit, the AutoScooper 12 arrived virtually fully assembled, and once Iâd unpacked the various components from their boxes or bags, I only needed to attach the legs, insert a liner into the waste tray, and attach the step to the front. Add some clumping bentonite-clay litter and presto! With a tray area of 12â x 14â, the AutoScooper 12 is quite a bit smaller than my 15â x 16â unit, but the actual litter volume capacity is quite similar, so this will only be an issue if you have particularly large cats.

Being naturally curious and experienced automatic litter box users, my cats wasted no time becoming intimately familiar with their shiny new toilet, and the AutoScooper 12 is even quieter than the one I already have! When given the option of using their old top-entry, enclosed litter box, all five cats chose the open-topped AutoScooper every time.

One thing I did notice is that while my other unit will pause mid-cycle if you look at it wrong, the AutoScooper 12 is not quite as sensitive. To allow waste storage, self-cleaning litter boxes are unavoidably tall, and I really like how the AutoScooperâs step latches onto the waste drawer. I particularly liked that the waste drawer came out the front, unlike my other unit where I have to shimmy things around to open it from the side.

If used on its own with a single cat, I would estimate that it would take at least 10-14 days for the waste drawer to register as full. However, it is recommended that you empty the drawer every 5-7 days, depending on conditions, to avoid odors, mould, and flies.

There were only a couple of things I was a bit bummed about with the AutoScooper 12. Not having an alternative litter guard option to allow the use of long-fiber cat litters like tofu is a shame, particularly as these more eco-friendly materials are becoming more popular.

Another slight design flaw is that litter and debris accumulate around the top of the tray where the liner meets the unit, and need to be dislodged with a brush.

Overall, I think the AutoScooper 12 from PetPivot is a really nice little unit, particularly for the price. It could be a tad small if youâve got a big Maine Coon or similarly large breed of cat, but for everyone else, the compact size means you wonât struggle to find space to accommodate it.

If youâre on the fence about getting a self-cleaning litter box, but arenât sure if your budget can stretch to such luxuries, itâs time to check out the AutoScooper 12 from PetPivot. Your cats deserve it, and so do you. And at this price, an automatic litter box isnât just wishful thinking; it belongs on next weekâs shopping list.

For most of us, however, these technological wonders have long been seen as luxury items that only the super-rich could afford.

The compact & stylish AutoScooper 12 proves that those days are well and truly over.

This self-cleaning litter box from PetPivot is quiet, easy to use, and is more than a match for units that cost five or six times its price. So unless you love the daily drudgery of scooping out the litter box, go out and treat yourself to an AutoScooper 12 â you wonât regret it.

#7829. My Husband Wants To Bring His Girlfriend To Thanksgiving. I’m Not Sure I’m Ready.

Just because we have an open relationship doesn’t mean I’m ready for such a big step.

Welcome to Ask A MWLTF (Yes, that’s Mother Who Likes to F*ck.), a monthly anonymous advice column from Scary Mommy. Here we’ll dissect all your burning questions about motherhood, sex, romance, intimacy, and friendship with the help of our columnist, Penelope, a writer and mental health practitioner in training. She’ll dish out her most sound advice for parents on the delicate dance of raising kids without sacrificing other important relationships. Email her at askpenelope@scarymommy.com.

My husband and I have been open for about two years. It was something we discussed carefully, and, for the most part, it has worked for us. We have rules, we communicate, and I’ve met a couple of the women he’s dated. I’m not interested in knowing every detail, but I also don’t feel threatened by the fact that he has relationships outside our marriage.

Now he’s been seeing someone for about six months, and he wants to bring her to Thanksgiving at my parents’ house.

We have two kids, and Thanksgiving is a big family holiday for us. My parents, siblings, nieces and nephews will all be there. My husband says he wants to stop treating this relationship like something that has to be kept separate from the rest of his life. He says he’s serious about her and thinks including her would make things feel more natural and less secretive.

I understand that. But I also feel strangely territorial. Thanksgiving is one of the few days of the year when I get to be with my whole family, and I don’t particularly want to spend it navigating my husband’s girlfriend. I’m worried about what my parents will think, what the kids will make of it, and whether I’ll spend the entire day feeling like I’m auditioning for the role of Cool, Secure Wife.

I don’t want to be controlling or make him feel ashamed of a relationship that I’ve agreed he can have. But I also don’t want to be pushed into a level of openness I haven’t agreed to. Am I being unreasonable?

It's easy for pressure to arise in a consensually non-monogamous relationship, and it often wears the very respectable outfit of personal growth. You have agreed to be open-minded, so shouldn’t you be open? You have agreed that your husband can love or desire other people, so shouldn’t you be comfortable meeting them? And if you’re not comfortable, does that mean you’re secretly jealous, insecure, or not as evolved as you thought you were?

No. It means you are a person with boundaries, and boundaries do not disappear just because you have made an unconventional relationship choice.

One of the more persistent misunderstandings about non-monogamy is that consent to one arrangement somehow implies consent to all the arrangements that might follow from it. But agreeing that your husband can date other people is not the same as agreeing that those people will become part of your family life. Being comfortable with his girlfriend existing is not the same as wanting her seated next to your Aunt Carol while everyone argues about the turkey.

These are different levels of intimacy. They involve different audiences, different risks, and different emotional demands. You can be genuinely supportive of your husband’s relationship and still want to keep Thanksgiving to the people who have traditionally been part of Thanksgiving.

In fact, I wonder if what you’re reacting to is not simply the presence of another woman, but the feeling that a boundary you thought was understood is being moved. Until now, your husband’s outside relationships have occupied a particular space in your marriage. They may be meaningful, even serious, but they have not been woven into the rituals that organize your family life. Bringing his girlfriend to Thanksgiving would change that. It would make the relationship visible to your parents and children, and it would ask you to participate in presenting it as part of the family.

That is a significant request. It deserves more than a casual, “Wouldn’t it be nice if she came?”

Your husband may have a legitimate desire to stop compartmentalizing. He may feel that keeping his girlfriend separate from his family life makes her seem less important, or that the secrecy itself is beginning to feel uncomfortable. Those feelings are worth taking seriously. But his desire for integration does not automatically create an obligation for you to provide it, particularly on a holiday that belongs to your family history as much as it belongs to your marriage.

And let’s talk about the children. There is nothing inherently harmful about children knowing that a parent has a romantic relationship with someone other than their spouse. But introducing a partner into family life is not a neutral logistical decision. It raises questions about what the children understand, what they have been told, what they might repeat to relatives, and whether the adults have a shared explanation. If your husband wants his girlfriend to be part of family gatherings, the two of you need to agree on what that means before you put a new person in the middle of a holiday and hope everyone figures it out over pie.

I would also encourage you to resist the temptation to make this a referendum on how good you are at non-monogamy. You do not have to prove your security by accepting every proposed next step. Sometimes the most honest thing you can say is, “I’m okay with your relationship, but I’m not ready for it to occupy this particular space in my life.”

That is not a punishment. It is information.

You might tell your husband something like: “I understand why you want the people in your life to know one another, and I’m not asking you to hide or minimize this relationship. But Thanksgiving with my family feels like too big a first step. I need us to talk about what integrating our relationships into family life would look like, and I don’t want to make that decision under pressure or on a holiday.”

Then get specific. Does he want you to meet her in a lower-stakes setting first? Does he imagine that she will attend future family events? Does he want the children to know about the relationship? What does she want? Is she comfortable being introduced to your parents as your husband’s girlfriend? And what happens if you discover that you like her, but still don’t want to share Thanksgiving with her? Or if you don’t like her? Or if your husband expects you to be warm and welcoming in a way that feels emotionally dishonest?

These are not small details. They are the actual relationship you’re negotiating.

There is another possibility worth considering: Your husband may be asking for something that sounds like inclusion but is, at least in part, a request for reassurance. Perhaps he wants to know that you accept his girlfriend, that he doesn’t have to split his life into separate compartments, that his happiness won’t always be experienced as a threat to your marriage. If so, you can offer reassurance without agreeing to this particular plan. You can say, “I don’t want you to feel ashamed of this relationship. I just don’t want to make Thanksgiving the place where we figure out how to live with it.”

And if he insists that your reluctance means you aren’t truly comfortable with non-monogamy, I would push back. A relationship agreement is not a blank check. It is an ongoing negotiation, and the terms can become more complicated as people’s feelings and circumstances change. You are allowed to discover that something you thought you could handle feels different when it moves from the abstract to the dining room.

So perhaps the question isn’t whether his girlfriend gets to come to Thanksgiving this year. It’s whether the two of you can talk about the future of your family life without either of you treating the other’s feelings as evidence of a moral failing. He should be able to tell you that he wants more integration. You should be able to tell him that you’re not ready. Neither of you gets to turn your preference into the only enlightened position.

And for what it’s worth, Thanksgiving is already a holiday with enough emotional labor, complicated family dynamics, and people pretending to enjoy casseroles they hate. You are not obligated to add a major relationship milestone to the menu.

You can take this one holiday at a time. The turkey will survive.

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling’s Christmas tree display is ever so chic, and ever so easy to make yourself using cuttings from your own garden...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are one of those celebrity couples that keep their heads down and their private lives just that; private. So sue us, then, that we get excited when they offer us a sneak-peek into their world... especially when it comes with a Christmassy twist!

Now, we usually think of a Christmas tree as being larger than life, and twice, especially when it's in the home of a celebrity. Honestly, though, most stars seem to be taking a laidback approach to their festive decor of late, whether it's the Beckhams' bow-filled Christmas tree, Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, or even Michelle Obama's twig tree.

Eva and Ryan have opted for a similarly unfussy approach; the couple's kitchen island is full of miniature Christmas trees. Check it out:

And just like that, they've proven you don’t need a large traditional evergreen tree to make your house look stylish during the holidays. In fact, if you decide to follow in Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's footsteps, you might not need to buy much at all.

All you have to do is take a simple stroll around your garden with a pair of pruners and a small pot to get the same look; fortunately, some experts told me exactly how to do it.

“The best mini Christmas trees start with a walk around your own garden,” says Nick Alan, founder of Palma Botanical Co., who has been growing plants for 25 years.

His picks? “Conifer tips like cedar, cypress, juniper and fir hold their needles longest. Boxwood and rosemary fill gaps and add scent.”

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

For clean cuts, Nick Alan recommends these Fiskars SoftGrip bypass pruners.

Use gentle hands with the shrub, though. “Harvest on a cool morning with clean pruners, cutting just above a side shoot so the plant regrows, and take no more than a third of any shrub,” says Alan.

Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a simple pot method for getting the Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling look this Christmas.

“Fill a 4-inch pot with damp sand (this will help hold your stems upright and will allow you to leave the tree in its pot as it dries). Remove the needles from the bottom 2 inches of each stem (you don’t want any foliage to rot in the sand!).”

Once this is done, she says you should “arrange the stems from tallest in the middle to shortest as you work your way out (creating a cone shape).” Remember, though, that cut foliage won’t last forever. “Mist every few days and keep it away from the stove, dishwasher vent, and sunny windows. Expect two to three weeks, swapping tired sprigs,” says Alan.

A living tree means you don’t have the extra work of worrying about sprigs. “For a kitchen island display like Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's, I like a living miniature tree best, because it does two jobs at once: it looks festive, and it stays useful after Christmas,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

Brooks says rosemary is the practical pick for a kitchen: “Rosemary is the most practical in a kitchen because you can pick sprigs for cooking, and it smells wonderful near the stove.”

For care, Brooks says: “I keep young trees in cool spots away from radiators and water the compost so it stays lightly damp but never wet.” Alan adds: “Give it your brightest window, water when the top inch is dry, and plant it out afterward in zone 8 and warmer.”

Your kitchen island may be a great spot for trees, but don’t forget it’s also a workspace for cooking. Keep your trees all to one side and never let them near heat sources, especially the dry foliage.

Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, says that “a little greenery with one beautiful ribbon often looks more considered than a crowded arrangement.”

For the layout, Melam says: “I love displaying mini trees in odd-numbered clusters of varying heights. Negative space is key! I’d keep the tallest stem 10-12 inches so as not to compete with faucets, etc.”

A tray helps too: “Displaying them on a tray or wooden slab can help tie them together & unify the display (as opposed to them looking like random pots on a counter).” On a budget, Alan says: “Pine cones, dried orange slices and ribbon dress them cheaply.”

Alan has one note of advice for people with pets or small children: “Skip holly, yew and mistletoe around pets and kids, since all are toxic.”

While Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling have both played a variety of characters throughout their film careers, we really do think that “people with a stunning Christmas kitchen island” is one we really fancy having a go at, too.

#7823. Rachael Leigh Cook Talks Her New Hallmark Rom-Com, Parenting Teens & 'She's All That'

The Double Booked for the Holidays star (and mom of two) opens up about being in the parenting-a-teen trenches with the rest of us.

For a whole generation of us, Rachael Leigh Cook will forever be Laney Boggs walking down those stairs in *the* red dress. But these days, in addition to being a busy working actor, she’s also a mom of a 13-year-old and an 11-year-old, which means she’s living through the tween and teen years like the rest of us. (“Mixed job performance reviews from my 13-year-old, for sure,” she admits.) And, yep, her daughter has even seen Cook’s iconic ‘90s movies like She’s All That. Her review? She’s glad her mom’s eyebrows grew back.

Also like so many of us, Cook’s a total sucker for a cozy holiday rom-com. It just so happens she’s currently starring in one: Double Booked for the Holidays, now streaming on Hallmark+. She plays identical twins Abigail and Charlie, who head to Wales to a bookish Airbnb for their first Christmas after losing their mom.

When we caught up with Cook, she filled us in on playing double duty, the “say yes” theory that led her to her boyfriend, and the ‘90s icons she considers go-to comfort watches.

Scary Mommy: You're playing twins, which means you're your own scene partner. Which sister is more you, Abigail or Charlie?

Rachael Leigh Cook: I think our producers thought of Abigail as the sort of anchor character in the story. Her love story gets a little bit more screen time, but I just related a lot more to the Charlie character. So that sort of just felt a little easier to latch onto and to have fun with because I'm always just trying to have the best time. When you make these movies, I feel like the audience's enjoyment is my responsibility. If the scene is informational, I'm going to try to make it go fast for you. If it could be a little bit silly, I'm going to make it as silly as they let me. I want it to be fun for you. So when I got to be Charlie and I felt like I got to deliver a little bit more razzle dazzle or whatever you want to call it, that's what felt the best.

SM: What did you do to make the twins feel different? Because I literally had to keep reminding myself there are not, in fact, two of you.

RLC: Julie, that's the nicest thing that you could say. That's what I was utterly terrified of. I read the script, and I thought, Uh-oh, this is going to just seem like I'm talking to myself if I'm not careful because I'm very guilty of being a multi-screen viewer. I'm not afraid to look at my phone. Those shows where if someone just looks at someone and it means something and then you don't understand the next scene, I'm lost. I can't handle it. So I knew that for people like me who might also drift off and just get a snack, I needed everything to be clear. I couldn't have people dipping in and out and feeling confused. This is a holiday movie. We're not trying to confuse anyone.

I really just tried to separate vocally and work from the top of my vocal range to the basement. And that's a little bit difficult because I realized that at the top I can't project very well. But other than that, I feel like it worked pretty well. I just tried to separate the physicality as much as I could so that people weren't confused. We realized that just because of the quick schedule we're on, I couldn't even change hair between the two very much. I got concerned pretty early on that it was just going to be a giant melting pot of too much of me, and that seemed just real bad. So I thought I got to just separate them as much as I can. And if I'm bad, I'm bad, but no one's confused.

SM: You once said something I loved, which is that you’re happiest to be alive when you're living wholly unique experiences.

SM: Did Christmas in a Welsh bookshop movie count?

RLC: Absolutely. I didn't even read the whole script before I said yes. I probably shouldn't admit that, but I just thought no one's going to call and ask if I want to play my own twin ever again in Wales. I can figure out the rest. I'll be fine. This is a say yes moment if there ever was one.

SM: For sure. Any other recent examples that made that list?

RLC: It was I think a little over a year and a half ago, but I remember this day because I got two back-to-back emails. And, listen, most days as an actor are things like, Yeah, they don't want you for that part or Oh, here's a two-cent residual check or whatever. It ain't all glamor.

But one day I got two back-to-back emails and one of them said, "Do you want to be a guest on Name That Tune?" And the other one right after it said, "Do you want to be in a float in the Hollywood Christmas Parade?" And I just wrote, "Yes, send, yes, send." And before I knew it, I had two completely wild experiences because of those things. Because of one of them, I met my now boyfriend, and because of the other one, I got to go and play Name That Tune with Michelle Williams from Destiny's Child.

So that was a pretty awesome validation of my say yes theory.

SM: I am obsessed with everything you just said. Also, that sounds like its own little mini Hallmark movie — you met your boyfriend?! Come on.

RLC: I mean, Hallmark can do just about no wrong as far as I'm concerned. They provide so much cortisol-free entertainment for people with wildly stressful jobs and lives, and I'm all about it. I'm drinking that Kool-Aid all day.

SM: Me too, sister. Well, I want to dip into some nostalgia because we actually recently put your She's All That dress on our list of pop culture dresses we were all obsessed with growing up. You’ve said it didn’t really change you, but rather it revealed your confidence. Do you have a real-life article of clothing that does that for you now?

RLC: I almost don't want to draw attention to it because I know that you'll then see how many times I've worn this. I have this great tracksuit by... Oh my gosh, I can't remember. Why can't I even remember who makes it? I got it in New York. It's sort of cranberry colored. It has stripes on the sleeves. I can get this information to you. And it's matching pants and a top, and there's almost nowhere that this set can't go because you can wear it with heels and some big jewelry and it feels very sort of casual, upscale, athleisure, or you can wear it with sneakers and no extra anything and it just looks like you put some thought into it.

That is my I don't know what to wear outfit. Everyone should have one of those.

SM: Oh, 100%. Well, I know you're in the thick of the tween and early teen years. I have a 13-year-old and a 15-year-old, so we're in it. Number one: how are you?

RLC: Thank you for asking. I think I'm doing fine, but yeah, mixed job performance reviews from my 13-year-old, for sure. I sometimes just feel like I can do no right, and it's really difficult. I'm trying to take what my friends with older kids say about, Oh, it's just because they feel so safe with you that they can just live as their frustrated self, and then they go to school and they behave well and toe the line and all of that. So I'm just like, yep, I'm so honored, so honored. It's a bumpy ride over here, but it's also the very best, and I wouldn't change a thing about it.

I'm absolutely horrified because I can see almost the first break of dawn's light far in the distance of them wanting to leave my home, and that is totally unacceptable. I'm like, "No, you have to stay my babies forever." My son is 11 and still doesn't love sleeping with all the lights off, so I'm hopeful that I can feel like I'm still the mom to a young child in some small ways anyway.

SM: Like you said, it's very day-to-day, so we're just rolling with it. But it's also cool to get to see more of who they're becoming, which I think is really fun.

RLC: Very well said. That's the incredible part. Even though it's the worst thing ever when those memory photos show up on your phone of them as a baby — it's painful because you can't have that time anymore — it's like, "Well, yeah, but I also didn't know you as well."

SM: Exactly. Your daughter, Charlotte, is 13 now… has she watched She’s All That or Josie and the Pussycats yet?

RLC: She has. And they came with me to a screening of Josie at the Hollywood Forever Cemetery pretty recently, and there were, I think, 4,000 people there. It was a big group, and I feel really grateful to them and the revival houses because I don't know if in this day and age there's any chance that my kids would be able to experience work I've done on that scale ever again. I think the kids were mostly in it for the candy, but they were very respectful.

I think my daughter said she's glad my eyebrows grew back, and so am I.

SM: Kids… they sure know how to keep you humble! Last question: As a ‘90s and early ‘00s icon, you’re a comfort watch for a lot of us.

SM: I’m curious, what is your comfort watch?

RLC: Oh, man. I geeked out over... I met Elizabeth Shue one time. I can't tell you how many times I've seen Adventures in Babysitting. So someone like that. I've never met Molly Ringwald, but I would be the least cool human in the world. I grew up on John Hughes movies and her. So yeah, I'd say those.

SM: I love it. You’ve been a true joy, and it's such an honor to meet you.

RLC: Mine! And you're doing great. You really are.

SM: You too. We’ll get to the other side of all this; we will.

SM: Oh, babe, that’s a convo for a whole other interview.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

What are the best diapers for a baby with sensitive skin? Look for diapers that are fragrance-free, hypoallergenic, and dermatologist-tested, ideally with third-party accreditation. What diapers do pediatric dermatologists recommend for sensitive or reactive skin? What’s the best hypoallergenic diaper for a baby with eczema? The National Eczema Association’s Seal of Acceptance is the clearest outside marker for eczema-prone skin and, according to the NEA, Pampers Pure Protection currently carries it.

What’s the best sensitive-skin diaper of 2026 for a baby with eczema? Pampers AMORE is the newest diaper built specifically for sensitive skin. Per Pampers, it’s accredited by the Skin Health Alliance, tested against more than 1000 chemicals, and free of fragrance, parabens, elemental chlorine, and latex.

Can switching diapers alone fix my baby’s eczema? No. A fragrance-free, hypoallergenic diaper helps, but routine matters as much or more: change every two to three hours, use barrier cream at every change, give daily diaper-free time, and clean gently. And since eczema is a chronic condition, your pediatrician should be part of the plan.

Why does my baby’s rash only show up near the diaper elastic or leg cuffs? That pattern suggests a contact allergy to dye or elastic material rather than just general dermatitis. Have your pediatrician take a look.

#7821. The Common Flea Pill Preventing New World Screwworm

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

For many cat parents, the brand Capstar might ring a bell. This small, fast-acting tablet has long been used to kill adult fleas on cats and dogs. Now, the active ingredient in Capstar, nitenpyram, is being given an important new role: treating and preventing New World screwworm.

On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA for nitenpyram tablets, allowing the common flea tablet to be used off-label for the prevention and treatment of New World screwworm infestations in cats, kittens, dogs, and puppies.

Why does this matter? Because until now, prevention was the missing piece when it came to drug options for dogs and cats. This new authorization helps fill that gap, giving veterinarians another tool in the toolbox while the larger fight against New World screwworm continues.

First things first: despite the rather dramatic name, New World screwworm is not a worm at all. It is a fly: Cochliomyia hominivorax. The âwormâ part of the name comes from the larvae, or maggot, of this fly. And unfortunately, this is one fly that definitely deserves our attention.

The trouble starts when a female fly finds a suitable place to lay her eggs, usually in or around a wound. She can also target other vulnerable areas, including the eyes, nose, mouth, and other mucous membranes. Once those eggs hatch, the larvae get to work, and this is where the screwworm becomes particularly nasty.

These aren't the disgusting but harmless little maggots that make themselves at home in overflowing trash cans or rotting food. Screwworm larvae feed on living tissue, burrowing deep into the affected area, feeding as they grow. Before long, a wound that looks small on the outside has become a much bigger problem underneath. An infestation can cause extensive tissue damage and, without prompt treatment, can even be life-threatening.

New World screwworm has been detected in the United States, while Mexico and other countries in the region continue to deal with the parasite. USDA is maintaining surveillance and response efforts, including in Texas, where âzones of infestationâ have been established.

The concern goes well beyond individual animals. Screwworm can have a serious economic impact on livestock production because affected animals may lose weight, require treatment and extra care, or die. During a 1976 outbreak in Texas, producers spent an estimated $132.1 million dealing with the pest, equivalent to about $740 million in 2024 dollars. More recently, the disruption to live cattle exports from Mexico has been estimated to have cost that country's livestock sector around $1.8 billion.

This is why so much effort is going into keeping this fly from spreading. This is about animal health, but it is also about protecting our entire food production system.

And no, the strategy is not simply âfind the bugs and squish them.â Controlling screwworm takes a much bigger effort. Authorities are using surveillance, movement controls, trapping, and other measures, along with one particularly interesting tool: releasing sterile flies.

The idea is surprisingly simple. Sterile male flies are released into affected areas, where they compete with fertile males for mates. When a sterile male mates with a female, she does not produce viable offspring. Over time, this can cripple the wild screwworm population.

The good news is that this isn't something every cat owner needs to panic about. Where a cat lives, where it travels, and whether it spends time in an area where screwworm is present all make a difference. For cats traveling to or returning from affected areas, it's worth being a little more careful.

With screwworm, the goal is to understand the risk before the exposure happens and, whenever possible, st ay one step ahead of the fly. When you consider that cats are experts at hiding things, including small wounds, a puncture, scratch, or other break in the skin can be easy to miss under all that fur, especially in an outdoor cat.

A wound can become an invitation for a female screwworm fly to lay her eggs, and the larvae that hatch will feed on living tissue. Cats infested with screwworm larvae have wounds that aren't healing normally, visible maggots, an unusual odor, or discharge. In any situation, these signs warrant veterinary attention. If you happen to live near or have traveled to an area where the New World screwworm has been detected, be sure to mention it to your vet.

Not necessarily. This does not mean Capstar should suddenly become part of every cat's routine parasite prevention. As a flea treatment, it is particularly effective at killing adult fleas quickly, but doesnât provide long-term flea control.

A cat living indoors in an area where screwworm isn't present is in a very different situation from a cat traveling to an affected region or spending time outdoors there. Your veterinarian can help you decide whether your cat's particular situation calls for the medication.

In the case of screwworm, Capstar is used according to the Emergency Use Authorization, not the FDA-approved standard use. There are specific instructions for when and how it should be given.

If you're traveling with your cat to an area where screwworm has been identified, or returning from one, talk with your veterinarian before you go. International travel can also come with health certificates, inspections, and other paperwork, and the requirements vary depending on the country you're entering or passing through. Some documents must be completed within a specific window before travel, so don't leave the paperwork until the last minute.

For most cats, New World screwworm is not something to worry about every day. But for cats living in or traveling to affected areas, knowing the risk, knowing that preventive options are available, and knowing what to look for can make a real difference. Itâs also great to know that those options include a product that has been safely used in cats for decades.

The takeaway isn't that every cat needs Capstar, but when a parasite like screwworm becomes a concern, having a preventive option available can make it easier to protect cats that are actually at risk.

And when a parasite feeds on living tissue, âbetter safe than sorryâ is a pretty good philosophy.

#7820. The Best Diapers For Diaper Rash, Ranked (2026)

If your baby’s bottom looks like a tomato by 3 p.m., the diaper matters as much as the cream.

If you’ve changed what feels like 400 diapers today, used enough cream to frost a sheet cake, and the rash is still winning, you’re not doing anything wrong. The good news is that rash-prone skin is super common, and it’s manageable. But (or butt, if you will) diaper rash prevention isn’t just about cream and wipes. The diaper matters too, and the best diapers for diaper rash handle moisture and let skin breathe. Turns out you don’t have to choose.

The one with actual clinical data behind it.

Why: In a Pampers-sponsored randomized trial published in Pediatric Dermatology in 2021, the Swaddlers and Sensitive Wipes regimen led to 50% fewer instances of severe redness and twice as many redness-free babies compared with other widely available options. Pampers also says Swaddlers also have Dual Leak-Guard Barriers, are hypoallergenic, and have been fragrance-free in every size since June 2026.

For the baby whose skin files a complaint about everything.

Why: Coterie says it uses TCF (totally chlorine-free) pulp, a manufacturer claim meaning no chlorine is used in processing, with no added fragrance, parabens, latex, or lotions.

For when the diaper budget is already doing a lot.

Why: Hello Bello says its plant-based diapers skip synthetic fragrances, lotions, and parabens.

For summers that feel like the inside of a diaper pail.

Why: Bambo Nature says these have a fully breathable backsheet, TCF pulp, and no fragrances or moisturizing lotions.

When newborn sizes still look like a parachute.

Why: Huggies says these have a wetness indicator and are hypoallergenic and free of fragrance, parabens, and elemental chlorine.

Because you’ll go through approximately one million of them.

Why: Costco says its store brand is hypoallergenic and dermatologically tested for sensitive skin, and comes in 160-count boxes for Size 1.

Should I get a more absorbent or a more breathable diaper to prevent rash?

Both. Absorbency keeps wetness off skin, and breathability lets heat and humidity escape. Look for a diaper that does both.

Is a fragrance-free or an extra-absorbent diaper better for preventing diaper rash?

You want both in one diaper. Fragrance-free cuts down on irritants, while absorbency handles the moisture behind a lot of rash.

Is it worth paying more for a rash-preventing diaper, and which one is best?

Not necessarily. Frequent changes and barrier cream often matter more than price. Pampers Swaddlers is our top pick, backed by a Pampers-sponsored study showing 50% fewer instances of severe redness, at a mainstream price.

What’s the best rash-preventing diaper for a preemie with delicate skin?

Preemie skin needs extra-gentle materials, frequent changes, and clinician guidance before you switch products. Pampers says its Swaddlers Preemie diapers were developed with NICU nurses, are fragrance-free and hypoallergenic, and come in sizes P3 to P1 for babies under about 6 pounds.

Is a wetness-indicator diaper or an extra-absorbent diaper better for preventing rash?
