#7817. Who’s a Scaredy Cat? Keeping Cats Safe This Halloween

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting new people.

The biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

Even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

Keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most important Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

With trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

Carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

Battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

It can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

Some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

Cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

It's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

However, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.

The red bracts get all the attention, but the little buds in the middle of a poinsettia say far more about its ability to last the distance over the holidays.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It happens every December. You bring home a full, bright red poinsettia, set it on the table, and a week or two later the colorful bracts start to curl and fall. By Christmas morning, the plant looks tired and half bare.

Some of that can be blamed on poinsettia care after you get home, like a cold windowsill or a pot left sitting in water. Much of it starts at the store, though. The plant was already on its way out before it ever went in the cart.

There's an easy way to tell a fresh one from a tired one, and hardly anybody looks. Forget the red for a second. Down in the center of each cluster of colored leaves are some tiny yellow-green buds, and those say a lot more about how long the color will hold up. It's kind of a strange thing to judge a plant by, but trust the process.

Those colorful "petals" on a poinsettia aren't petals at all. They're bracts, and they color up in fall as the nights get longer. Right in the middle sit the real flowers, small knobby clusters called cyathia. Each one is a little cup holding a single female flower and several male flowers, often with a yellow gland on its rim.

Cyathia go through the same cycle on every plant. They start out tight and green or red-tipped, open to shed yellow pollen, and then drop off. After the cyathia fall, the colored bracts usually follow before long.

Some of the newer poinsettia varieties hang on to their cyathia longer. So it isn't a sure thing, but it's still one of the better clues you get in the store. Any color works for this check, whether you're eyeing red or the pink poinsettias at Walmart (which come in a four-pack for maximum festive joy).

Bend down and look closely at the center of a few bracts. Plants on the same table can be at different stages, so check more than one. Ideally, the cyathia are mostly closed, green or tipped with red, and fresh-looking. Some yellow showing is fine on its own. That's often just the gland on the side of the cup – it doesn't mean the flower has opened.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Now compare that to a plant where the buds have split open and yellow pollen is dusting the bracts below them. If you see that, or you find bare stubs where cyathia used to be, that poinsettia has been blooming a while already. It may look fine today, but it has less time left than the one beside it with tight buds.

Classic red poinsettias come in a four-pack from Costa Farms, and you can order them on Amazon – and the same quick look at the center works on a plant that shows up at the door.

The green leaves under the bracts deserve a look too. Check for yellow leaves low on the stems, or bare spots where leaves have already dropped. Cold, poor light, and watering trouble can all cause that. Pass on a plant that droops or looks wilted, along with any that have torn, bruised, or creased bracts. Bluish or whitish edges on the bracts can be a sign of cold injury.

Flip a few leaves over as well. Whiteflies, such as the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), are common on poinsettias, and a puff of tiny white insects lifting off when you brush the plant is a bad sign.

Lift the pot if you can. Soggy soil in a heavy pot may mean it's been sitting in water inside its foil, and roots kept that wet can rot. Pay attention to where the plants are displayed, too. Poinsettias crowded by the automatic doors can catch a blast of cold air every time the doors open, and plants left packed in plastic sleeves for days can droop and drop their flowers early – ethylene gas builds up inside the sleeve.

When you get home, use a soil moisture meter, like the Xlux moisture meter available on Amazon, to take the guesswork out of watering.

The journey home is where poinsettias tend to get hurt. When it's below 50°F (10°C) outside, sleeve or wrap the plant before it leaves the store, even for the short walk to the car. Just a few minutes of cold air can damage the bracts and leaves, and the damage may not show right away. Save the garden center for your last stop so the plant isn't stuck in a cold car while you're in other stores, and warm the car up first. Once you're inside, get the sleeve off pretty quickly.

Pick a bright room for your poinsettia. Keep the plant near a window but out of hard, direct sun, and well clear of heat vents, the fireplace, and any door that lets in a draft.

Normal house temperatures work fine, roughly 65 to 70°F (18 to 21°C) during the day, with nights around 60°F (16°C) or a little warmer. Window glass gets cold at night, though, and so can the air right beside it. Set a digital indoor thermometer, like the TempPro TP50, for a night or two, and you'll know for sure.

Stick a finger in the pot before you water. If the top of the soil is dry, go ahead, and if it's still damp, wait a day or so. That shiny foil holds water like a bowl, so poke a few holes in the bottom, or take the pot out and water it over the sink until it drains. A ceramic planter, like this Garden & Home Red 8 Inch Indoor Ceramic Plant Pot, with drainage holes and saucer, is a much nicer option than foil anyway. You don't need fertilizer while a poinsettia is in bloom.

Pick a plant with tight little buds in the center, keep it somewhere warm and bright, and the color can hold for weeks after the holidays. So the next time you're standing in front of a whole table of red, skip past the brightest one for a second and look at the center first.

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, hosts Nicole and Dr. Karyn jump into an unstructured, wide-ranging discussion covering quirky pet habits, feline anatomy, and the ethics of animal testing vs. clinical research. From explaining the post-poop "zoomies" to reflecting on how decades-old feline nerve studies shed light on why cats freeze in harnesses, the hosts offer a lighthearted yet insightful look into how our pets interact with the world.

Discover the fascinating science behind feline movement, including how lower-body nerve pathways allow cats to adjust their bodies instinctively without waiting for brain signals. Dr. Karyn also breaks down why putting a coat or harness on a cat disrupts this "sixth sense," causing them to initially freeze or flop over.

Additionally, the hosts explore the difference between historical animal testing and modern, mutually beneficial clinical trials. From discussing how research into feline coronavirus treatments surprisingly overlapped with human health developments to debating why testing food or drugs on animals can be unreliable (imagine if chocolate was banned because it was tested on dogs!), this episode balances fun pet owner anecdotes with fascinating veterinary science.

The Mystery of "Poop Zoomies": Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how cats often sprint out of the litter box after taking a poop. They discuss how this hilarious habit stems from a mix of wild instinct (running from scent markers) and sheer physical relief.

Do Cats Always Land on Their Feet?: While cats try to land on their feet using their incredible spinal flexibility, Dr. Karyn notes it isn't an absolute ruleâpointing out that her own cat, Clutch, occasionally falls right on his butt.

How Feline Nerves Act Like a "Body Brain": Dr. Karyn discusses an old study on feline nerve pathways showing that cats can walk on a treadmill via spinal reflexes without upper brain input. This ultra-fast neural feedback gives cats rapid spatial awareness.

Why Cats Freeze in Harnesses: Because a cat's body relies heavily on sensory feedback from skin and nerves for orientation, placing clothes or a harness on them is like "blindfolding" their body, causing them to temporarily lose balance until they adapt.

Testing vs. Clinical Trials: The hosts differentiate between harmful animal testing and ethical clinical research. Modern veterinary trials often involve treating pet patients with naturally occurring conditions (like cancer or coronavirus), generating medical advancements that aid both humans and animals.

Interspecies Differences in Testing: The hosts touch on why testing human items on animals can be flawed, pointing out that many things safe for humans (like chocolate, grapes, or garlic) are toxic to pets, and vice versa.

#7812. 21 Holiday Gifts To Shop For Now So You Can Enjoy Them All Season Long

From custom wrapping paper to cozy matching PJs, these are the gifts worth grabbing before the December scramble.

If there’s one thing that’s wildly helpful to keep in mind heading into this final stretch of the year, it’s that the holidays aren’t just one day.

Right now, we’re in the warm-up period, getting ready for what’s ultimately a months-long marathon of hosting, gift-wrapping, card-writing and cozy holiday cheer. So while, sure, there may be bags of half-eaten Halloween candy currently littering your countertops, it’s time to start thinking about the stuff you need to do (and buy) now to max out the holiday merriment and minimize the holiday stress.

What most of us have learned the hard way, of course, is that personalized gifts need a little extra time to make and ship. Placing those orders now gives you the head start you need! But also, why save all the good stuff for December anyway? We here at Scary Mommy are big believers in gifting early, both to ourselves and the people we love, especially when it’s stuff that’ll get used all season long, like matching PJs for every hot cocoa night and puzzles to work on as the weather turns.

We’ve rounded up what we’re buying now so that the holidays can be more about the fun stuff and less about the December scramble.

I love the idea of giving personalized wrapping paper at the holidays. It's charming, it's unique, and it's very specific. When else would you do this — and actually use what you buy? — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief

These are very chic little cocktail napkins that make a great hostess gift throughout the holiday season. They come in a variety of patterns, and while, sure, are more than I normally spend on such a thing, they make a nice gift whether you're headed somewhere for cocktails, for Thanksgiving, or beyond. — Kate Auletta

Forgive me, but I'm at the age where I have more than one doormat. I even have a Halloween one outside right now. It spruces up your outdoor space in a second and makes a nice gift too. I just love coming home to a welcoming doormat; sue me. — Kate Auletta

If I had a nickel for every personalized notebook I had... I'd have about $3. But still, the point remains: A personalized notebook makes a great gift. You remember who gave it to you as you open it to start using it, and, as someone who is a chronic pen-and-paper girlie, I just love them. They make a great gift year-round, but especially at the holidays. — Kate Auletta

I have a love-hate relationship with tree skirts. They're incredibly annoying, but incredibly useful. But I do love a tree skirt with character, and this one has it in spades. I love the idea of giving a newborn family a monogrammed tree skirt they can use for years to come. Such a sweet gift! — Kate Auletta

I'm a puzzler, especially when it gets cold outside. I love the idea of doing a thick wood, personalized puzzle that will remind you of the moment captured, as well as the person or family who gave it to you. It makes a lovely gift, promise. — Kate Auletta

Ok, how friggin' cute is this? My kids no longer believe in Santa, but I almost want to buy this for our house. It's a great thing to whip out as the holidays — and the gift requests — amp up. Read their letters and write personalized notes on Christmas Eve while drinking eggnog. Win-win. — Kate Auletta

I care about my guest bath maybe more than I care about my own. It's, like, my space. As such, I love the idea of giving monogrammed towels for the space that you can whip out, especially at the holidays. They'll get used, and they're great quality. — Kate Auletta

Call me a Boomer, but I love switching out throw pillows for each season. And I adore these tree pillows, which are not only affordable but can sit prettily on your couch for months. They're a lovely gift, or if you're feeling selfish, a lovely gift to yourself. — Kate Auletta

Any house that can pull off an outdoor lights display at the holidays is fine by me. What I love about these is that, sure, you can buy them for the winter holidays, but you can reuse them for Halloween, the Fourth of July, or a random Saturday. They're just so fun, especially if you have kids. You can't go wrong. — Kate Auletta

One of my absolute most favorite holiday traditions is seasonal PJs! When our kids were little, we would always get them matching sets like these super festive, cozy ones from Magnetic Me. The fact that these feature magnets for easy, over-the-head dressing is a huge bonus. Buy them now so you can be cute and coordinated for every holiday movie night and hot cocoa sipping session. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

White Christmas stans, rise! Old World Christmas hand-blown glass ornaments are genuinely heirloom quality, with that gorgeous old-fashioned detailing and rich color that makes them look like they came from a European Christmas market rather than an online cart. This one is specifically for sisters, which makes it an incredibly thoughtful gift for a sibling, a best friend who is basically a sister, or honestly just yourself if you have a sister you want to think of every time you see it on the tree. The kind of ornament that starts a tradition and gets passed down eventually! — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

We have had so much fun with our mini photo printer from Canon — and it's a perfect thing to get before the holidays get rolling. I love taking pictures during a party or event and then handing out hard copies as our guests go out the door. It's such a good, simple party favor. You can also set up homemade photo booths! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

Do yourself a favor TODAY and buy this Slice tool for cutting wrapping paper. I swear it saved me 7-10 business days while wrapping. I literally hide it from the rest of my family. And while you're at it, buy the Slice box cutter, too. They both make my life easier and happier. — Sarah Aswell

Before the turkey is steaming on your holiday table... before you need to chop one thousand vegetables for the party, run every knife in your kitchen through this electric knife sharpener. I bring this baby out right before the holidays start and sharpen everything that isn't nailed down in my kitchen, and it almost feels like self-care. Using a sharp knife makes so much more of a difference than you think! — Sarah Aswell

This is what I've been looking for! I love having cafe lights strung up around my porch for entertaining during the summer — what if they could just MAGICALLY turn into holiday lights for Halloween and then Christmas? Now they can. These programmable lights mean that I am not constantly putting up and taking down lights — the colors just change with the season, in whatever configuration you'd like. — Sarah Aswell

Nothing gets me and my house in the holiday mood quite like having a few really nice candles ready to go. I stay away from the sweeter smells of Christmas and gravitate for ones like this: evergreen and forest smells that are bright and crisp and cheery (even if you opt for a fake tree for your house). — Sarah Aswell

This combines so many of my interests: puzzles, national parks, and advent calendars! I love that this one involves an activity and that it doesn't result in a bunch of cheap junk in your house that never leaves. — Sarah Aswell

I love holiday cards, but actually writing them and addressing the envelopes can start to feel like too much of a task, especially with all the other stuff going on around the holidays. I love putting all of my cards, stamps, pens, and stickers in this little case and carrying it with me — I can get a few cards done wherever I am, whether it's my kid's ballet lessons, a doctor's waiting room, or a lunch alone. — Sarah Aswell

I am really trying to focus my holiday season around activities and togetherness over material things. One great way to do this is to get a few new board games that are super family-friendly. I love this one because it is still playable for kids on the younger side, but it's fun for adults, too. It's also just really pretty and magical and fun — you create lovely worlds with cool animals, for points of course. — Sarah Aswell

Before the holidays start, get yourself a go-to party dress that you can throw on without thinking for whatever occasion. My favorite this season is this dress by Body by Miraclesuit in dark green. You can literally just throw it on and run out the door, and yet it looks so pretty and flattering. And like any good holiday dress, you can elevate it really easily with some heels and jewelry or dress it down with a cardigan and flats. — Sarah Aswell

Wasps seem to vanish once the cold sets in, but not all of them are gone. Next year's queens are tucked away close by, and a few of their hiding spots might surprise you.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After the first hard frost, the wasps that pestered every picnic in August are suddenly gone. It's easy to figure the cold finished them off. So where do wasps go in winter, and do wasps die in winter at all? Most of them do – just not the ones that count for next year.

Before you look up how to kill wasps next spring, know that yellowjackets, paper wasps, and hornets live in colonies that last just one season. Each colony leaves behind young queens that have already mated and will ride out the cold on their own.

Some of the places where wasps hide in winter are right in your yard. Firewood, loose bark, and the gaps around a shed door can each hold a queen until spring.

For the common social wasps, the colony only lasts a year. Each spring, a single queen starts a small nest and raises the first workers herself. The colony grows through summer, and by late summer it switches to raising males and new queens. The new queens mate in fall, then leave the nest for good.

Everyone else is left behind. By the time hard freezes settle in, the old queen, the workers, and the males have died, and the papery nest sits empty for good. The mated queens are the only ones that make it into winter, and they don't go back to the nest. Each one finds its own sheltered spot. Many still won't last until spring, but the ones that do will start the whole thing over.

Here are some of the common places you'll find queens hiding.

Rake back a deep drift of oak leaves in midwinter, and the ground underneath is often softer and less frozen than the open lawn. Yellowjacket queens may crawl into that leaf litter or under old mulch and pulled plants at the edge of a bed. They stay perfectly still. You'd likely never notice one. Some leaves left in place also help butterflies and moths overwinter, and there's no reason to rake every corner bare because of wasps.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Stacked firewood is full of narrow gaps out of the wind, and rotting logs and old stumps offer soft wood a queen can tuck into. Pull a few splits from the bottom of the stack in winter, and you may find one clinging to the bark, too cold to move much. Check each piece before carrying it inside – a warm living room can wake a dormant queen. Bring in only what you'll burn that day. Walmart's leather palm work gloves are tough enough for sorting through the stack.

Loose bark on a dead tree makes a snug pocket. Yellowjacket queens squeeze into those gaps. Birds have a hard time reaching them there, and the bark keeps off most of the weather. On a mild winter day, try lifting a slab of it off an old stump. You could find a queen pressed flat in the gap underneath, barely moving. Put the bark back if you do. She isn't going anywhere until spring.

Sheds, garages, and barns are full of cracks around door frames and window trim. Queens often move in during fall and stay put until spring. Paper wasps tend to seek out high spots for the winter, and they sometimes overwinter in clusters, packed together at the peak of a roof or along a rafter. To keep queens from slipping in next fall, cover open vents with stainless steel mesh, which Amazon sells in small sheets.

Queens find their way into wall voids and attics through gaps where siding meets trim, or through cracks around windows. Temperatures in there usually stay above freezing. Ever find a slow, groggy wasp on a window inside the house in January? It's usually a lone queen that wandered in from the walls, drawn toward the light. An active nest looks different – steady traffic in and out of the same hole in summer or early fall points to a live colony inside the wall.

Don't plug that hole while the nest is active, since the wasps may chew through to the inside. Once the colony has died off, seal exterior cracks with a flexible sealant such as DAP Dynaflex 230 from Home Depot.

Some yellowjacket queens spend the winter underground, but not in the nest they came from. That old nest is abandoned when the colony dies, and it isn't used again. She might use an empty mouse or vole burrow instead, a crack between rocks, or a small pocket in loose soil.

A home compost pile that hasn't been turned in a while is another possibility. If you turn the pile in winter, move slowly and wear gloves, and she'll probably stay put.

Usually, there's no need. Wasps are useful predators. Yellowjackets and paper wasps hunt caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects to feed their young, and the adults visit flowers for nectar, moving some pollen around as they go. A queen sleeping under a log at the back of the yard poses little risk, and next summer her colony will probably eat a good number of garden pests.

Doors, windows, and play areas are a different story. Seal gaps around the house in late summer, before queens go looking for winter shelter, and check that window screens fit tightly. Home Depot carries a door jamb weatherstrip set that closes the gaps around exterior doors.

Once spring warms up, glance at the eaves and porch ceiling every so often. A brand-new nest is about the size of a golf ball, and only the queen is tending it, so it's far easier to handle than a full colony in August. Large nests, ground nests, and anyone in the house who's allergic to stings are a job for a pest control professional.

In winter, the yard looks empty, but not entirely. Somewhere under those leaves or behind that bark, next year's wasps are sitting out the cold. Unless one is tucked in beside the back door, it can stay right where it is.

#7809. The Woman Keeping Pets and People Together | Heroes of the Pet World

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

As we drove through the beautiful mountain scenery surrounding Lake Chapala, I wasnât sure what to expect. Julie Wittmann picked me up early in the morning, and now we were on our way to help distribute food to families who needed extra help feeding their pets.

When we arrived, large sacks of cat and dog food had already been divided into individual portions by a team of Pet Food Bank Lakeside volunteers who gather every week to prepare the food for distribution. We moved the bags into two piles, one for each community they would serve, ready to be collected by volunteers who would take them to families in need.

It was simple work, but it was part of a much greater effort.

Pet Food Bank Lakeside is an independent partner of FoodBank Lakeside, which provides âdespensasâ (bags of basic groceries and household essentials) to families experiencing financial hardship. Families receiving assistance are asked how many pets they have, helping connect the two programs. The pet food program now provides food for more than 1,200 dogs and cats each month.

Next, Julie and I headed to the small town of Santa Cruz, joined by FoodBank Lakeside leader Steve Motenko, his wife Karen, their granddaughter, her best friend, and Javier, a cheerful local with a kind heart. Javier knows the families in the community and helps coordinate the deliveries.

Everyone we met was struggling financially. For most, that hardship was compounded by illness, age, or disability. We met a woman who was completely blind and several people who used wheelchairs.

Just like us, many have pets, and just like our own cats and dogs, theirs are companions, confidants, and cherished members of the family. For some of the people we met, who spend much of their time at home because of age or a health condition, their pet may be their most constant companion.

Looking at them, it was impossible to see a dog or cat as simply another expense. These animals were part of the family. They brought comfort, protection, affection, and, very often, a little joy into lives that could use more of it.

That is something Julie and FoodBank Lakeside understand well. Helping someone feed their pet is not just about putting food in a bowl. It is about helping preserve a very important relationship.

As we moved from house to house, we also carried treats for the dogs we met along the way. They quickly learned that the cars arriving meant something good was coming.

One particularly enthusiastic dog decided not to wait for us at home. He followed our cars from one house to the next, keeping pace for two or three stops as if he had appointed himself our unofficial escort.

It was a small, funny moment in an otherwise emotional morning, and it brought plenty of smiles from everyone.

What I noticed most was how happy most of these people were to see the volunteers arrive.

These were not strangers arriving at a doorstep with a bag of food. There were smiles, conversations, and a sense of familiarity that comes from years of showing up for the same community.

One of the women who had received help from the FoodBank for her cat had passed away only days before we arrived. Karen told me through tears that they had known each other for six years and had become very close. She described her as one of the sweetest women she had known.

The friendship had grown both ways. Over the years, the woman had prepared plant cuttings for Karen and given her handmade embroidery pieces as Christmas gifts. These were small gestures, but they spoke of a relationship that had grown far beyond a food delivery.

Her cat was still there, and the womanâs daughter was relieved to know that the pet food program would continue to help care for it.

I found that moment difficult to forget. The woman was gone, but the connections she had made remained in Karen's memories, in the plants she had shared, in the handmade gifts she had given, and in the cat still waiting at home.

That is something you cannot measure in bags of food, but in kilos of love instead.

Julie did not set out to create a large pet food program.

After moving from Portland, Oregon, to the Lake Chapala area, she began looking for ways to help animals in her new community. When COVID-19 disrupted daily life, she asked local veterinarians what they believed was needed most.

Local rescue groups were also concerned that families who could no longer afford to feed their dogs might eventually have to surrender them or turn them loose.

Julie started small. She bought large 25-kilogram bags of food, repackaged them herself, and drove into local communities to distribute them. As local groups organized despensas for families in villages around Lake Chapala, Julie saw an opportunity to make sure the pets were not forgotten. Over time, that small effort became Pet Food Bank Lakeside.

A partnership with FoodBank Lakeside allowed the program to reach more families. FoodBank Lakeside already knew which households were struggling and how many pets they had. The two programs could work together to help both people and animals.

Today, Julie has a community of volunteers helping with the work that she once did herself. In its six-year update, Pet Food Bank Lakeside reported more than 20 volunteers and the ability to prepare a month's supply of food in under two hours.

Julie and her volunteers also visit local schools to teach children about pet care.

For Julie, education is one of the most important ways to prevent animals from being misunderstood or mistreated.

âEducating children is particularly important,â Julie explains. âWhen they understand that the weird-looking dog has scabies, and that what it needs is medication, we prevent that dog from being mistreated and left aside.â

Her point is simple. Children need to understand what they are seeing before they can respond with compassion.

She sees the same principle in the way children learn what animals need.

âThe only way for kids to understand that it is not normal for dogs to spend all day tied up to a post is to let them know that this is not normal, to teach them what dogs are, what they need, and how they can enrich each other's lives.â

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

During our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

He describes Julie as admirable and says she has done an extraordinary amount to help pets in the Lakeside community.

After spending a morning with her, I understood why.

What struck me was that these deliveries were about so much more than food. They were about people knowing, caring for, and looking out for one another.

Javier knew the families. Karen had formed a six-year friendship with one of the women we visited. Volunteers gathered each week to prepare food. Teenagers came along to help. Julie kept showing up for the pets.

Julie says it simply: âWe believe food scarcity shouldn't separate families from their pets.â

After spending that morning with her, I understood that belief in a more personal way.

When someone is already struggling to afford food, dealing with illness, or living with a disability, feeding a pet can seem like one more impossible responsibility. But for the people we met, their animals were not disposable. They were very important companions, bringing comfort and connection to lives that were often anything but easy.

Helping them keep those animals fed also helped them keep an important part of their lives.

By the end of the day, I felt an enormous admiration for Julie and for the people who have joined her in this work.

I had arrived thinking I was just going to help deliver pet food. Instead, I witnessed something much bigger. I saw people who had built genuine relationships with their neighbors. I saw volunteers giving their time week after week. I saw teenagers learning to help others. I saw a daughter relieved that her mother's cat would continue to receive food.

Most of all, I saw how much a small act of kindness can mean when someone is having a difficult time.

My heart felt very warm on the drive home.

I kept thinking about those bags of food we had divided into two piles that morning.

At first, they had simply looked like bags of pet food waiting to be delivered.

By the end of the day, I understood what they represented.

And, sometimes, the chance for a person and the animal they love to stay together.

#7807. The Best Carpet Cleaners of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Amber Guetebier, Michelle Larson, Debbie Wolfe, Additional research provided by Timothy Dale

Published Nov 23, 2026 8:17 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

For an active household with lots of foot or paw traffic, a carpet cleaner, sometimes called a carpet shampooer, can make quick work of cleaning common stains and refreshing dingy rugs or carpets. Whether you’ve considered one for spot cleaning or need more frequent whole-house cleaning, carpet cleaners can make upkeep a lot easier.

We tested 23 top-rated carpet cleaners on rugs, carpets, and stairs to find which ones leave flooring fibers looking like new while also offering the best value. Our favorite was the Hoover SmartWash+ Automatic Carpet Cleaner thanks to its effective stain removal and overall cleaning power. Read on to find out why we also consider the following to be some of the best carpet cleaners on the market and learn about what features will best suit your home and lifestyle.

Whether you’re looking for a portable option for quick spot-cleaning or an upright for whole-house cleaning, our list has you covered. See how each carpet and rug cleaner we recommend fared in our tests and which one might be best for your needs.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Suction 5/5; Portability 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

With no buttons to push or triggers to pull, Hoover’s high-tech SmartWash+ carpet cleaner makes quick and easy work of messy tasks. Pushing the unit forward automatically turns on the cleaning function, and pulling it back switches the machine to auto-dry. The cleaner’s AutoMix system combines and dispenses the correct amount of carpet cleaner solution​, while the 1-gallon tank provides ample capacity for washing and rinsing.

In testing, it only took a few passes to remove all the test stains from our carpet square and get it bone dry. We found the dry-only mode especially helpful—so much so that we even used it on a couple of other still-wet test squares and pulled out an impressive amount of excess moisture. In addition to being easy to use and effective, this upright carpet-cleaning machine was lighter than similar models, which made it easier to maneuver and carry. With its longer power cord, 8-foot hose, and several attachments (including one for pet hair), it’s also quite versatile.

The downsides of this otherwise great machine were build quality and a not-always-intuitive design. Some plastic pieces came loose when we removed the hose, and we struggled to get them back into place. Also, after we took off the brush and cover for cleaning, they weren’t super easy to snap back on. Still, those issues felt minor compared to the overall value of this very effective carpet cleaner.

What our tester says: “It took us a little while to get used to the lack of buttons and triggers, but once we used the machine for a bit, we found it to be one of our favorites.”—Amber Guetebier, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Hoover SmartWash+ carpet cleaner at Amazon or Target.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Suction 4.5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4/5

This budget-friendly Hoover model is a whole-home carpet cleaner with a user-friendly compact design. It weighs just 12.5 pounds, making it ideal for anyone with limited storage space, yet the 0.5-gallon tank provides enough water for most rooms. This unit also features Hoover’s HeatForce Technology, which heats the carpet as dirty water is sucked into the tank for faster drying. It comes with a pet brush roll that helps collect hair and purge difficult stains, and though it doesn’t have a hose attachment, its low profile lets users get under furniture fairly easily.

This compact upright cleaner impressed us with how quickly it removed carpet stains, eliminating them in three passes, which took less than 5 minutes. After running it for another 2 minutes without dispensing any more water, our carpet square was dry to the touch. Though it was fast and very easy to use, the fact that it doesn’t come with an attachment hose made getting into small spaces and corners a little difficult. Also, compared to others, the process of removing the dirty water was a little awkward, but not enough to be a deal-breaker, especially at this price point. If you’re in the market for a carpet cleaner machine that gets the job done with no fuss and at a great price, this is an excellent choice.

Get the Hoover PowerDash carpet cleaner at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Effectiveness 4.3/5; Suction 5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4.7/5

The Bissell Little Green portable carpet and upholstery cleaner is a versatile machine designed to tackle everything from stained carpets to sticky auto interiors. Its powerful suction capabilities can efficiently remove messes from almost any soft surface, yet it’s small enough to carry from place to place without any hassle. The Little Green comes with two 48-ounce water tanks (one for clean water and one for dirty) that are easy to remove and maintain, a 3-inch tough-stain tool, a HydroRinse attachment, and a sample-size bottle of the brand’s cleaning solution.

In testing, this carpet spot cleaner​ easily eliminated dirt and fresh stains, and it greatly improved the appearance of set-in stains. We liked its large-capacity tanks, which reduced the frequency of filling and emptying, as well as its lightweight build and 15-foot cord for portability. And given how much of a pain it typically is to clean the hoses on carpet cleaners, the HydroRinse self-cleaning tool made it much easier to get the job done without spilling water everywhere.

Read our full review: Bissell Little Green Portable Carpet Cleaner

Get the Bissell Little Green carpet cleaner at Amazon, Ace Hardware, The Home Depot, Wayfair, or Bissell.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Suction 4/5; Portability 4.5/5; Value 4.6/5

With its low price and solid performance, Kenmore’s RevitaLite portable carpet cleaner gave our best bang for the buck winner a run for its money. However, given this budget-friendly model’s light weight and incredibly long hose and cord, it’s an easy win for the best carpet cleaner for stairs. Whether you’re in need of whole-house or spot cleaning, it does an excellent job removing everyday dirt as well as set-in stains.

In testing, this lightweight carpet cleaner​ was one of the easiest upright models to push and pull, likely because its clean and dirty water tanks sit quite low on the unit. Even with the 3.2-liter water tank full, it weighed just over 25 pounds, which helped a lot when maneuvering around furniture feet and up stairs.

While it only comes with two tools (a 3.5-inch tough stain tool and a 6.5-inch wide path tool), we found they were enough for everything from pulling up pet messes to getting old stains out of couch pillows. If we had one complaint, it’s that it didn’t seem to pull out as much extra moisture as others, which left the carpet a bit damp. A storage mat would be nice for catching post-cleaning drips, but for the price, it’s really a pretty minor issue.

What our tester says: “This was my favorite carpet cleaning machine for stairs, which is where our carpet tends to get the dirtiest. With the 8-foot hose and the 25-foot cord, I had no issue reaching the bottom steps from the ground floor and the top steps from the second.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Kenmore carpet cleaner at Amazon or Kenmore.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.7/5; Effectiveness 4.6/5; Suction 5/5; Portability 4.5/5; Value 4.4/5

The Shark CarpetXpert HairPro is an excellent pet stain carpet cleaner​ for those needing regular hair removal and targeted carpet deep cleaning. Designed to capture three times more pet hair and deliver 20 times more stain-removing power than traditional models, it’s ideal for ongoing carpet and rug maintenance as well as more urgent issues. In our tests, it was easily one of the best for picking up pet hair without clumping, and we loved that the brush roll was designed to prevent hair wrapping, which made post-use maintenance much easier.

This Shark couldn’t have arrived at a better time. Given that both of our dogs were sick for several days, we had ample opportunities to use all four attachments, including the pet mess extractor, 3.5-inch pet stain eliminator, mini stain eliminator, and hair extractor. In addition to tackling mess after mess, it was also easy to use thanks to a dual-tank design that automatically mixed Shark’s Deep Clean Pet and Oxy Multiplier cleaning solutions as needed. The LED warning lights let us know when the dirty water tank required emptying, and given the substances we were handling, we especially appreciated the hose’s self-rinse feature.

What our tester says: “One of our pets always seems to be sick when I’m testing carpet cleaners, and it happened again this time. But between the Shark’s pet mess attachment and powerful suction, you’d never know that both our pups have had a bug for the last 3 days.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Shark carpet cleaner at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Best Buy.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Suction 5/5; Portability 3/5; Value 4.5/5

This heavy-duty carpet cleaner from Bissell uses an extra-large rotary brush to lift dirt and deliver results similar to those of professional carpet cleaning. Its 1.75-gallon clean water tank holds more than enough water for most rooms, and the 9-foot hose reaches easily under beds, sofas, and other hard-to-access areas. The Big Green Pet Pro also comes with a pet stain tool and a 6-inch stair tool, but since it weighs 44 pounds, it can be hard to maneuver and requires significant storage space.

That size did offer much in the way of effectiveness, however. In just 20 minutes, we removed all the stains on our test squares plus several older spots on our low-pile basement carpet we thought would never come out. Its powerful 12-amp motor provided enough strong suction to leave our carpets surprisingly dry to the touch and completely dry within about 4 hours.

We also appreciated the cleaner’s practical attachments. The stair tool was great for corners and narrow areas, and the 6-inch attachment cleaned couch stains in under a minute. Anyone looking to avoid renting a carpet cleaner or paying to have their carpets professionally cleaned won’t be disappointed with this deep-clean carpet cleaner​.

Get the Bissell Big Green carpet cleaner at Amazon, Wayfair, Walmart, or Bissell.

The Tineco Carpet One Cruiser is a smart carpet cleaner that automatically adjusts suction power, water flow, and brush speed based on detected soil levels. Weighing just under 22 pounds with a 21-foot cord and low-set water tanks, it’s designed to be easy to maneuver for whole-house cleaning. It also comes with a two-in-one nozzle for maintaining carpet and upholstery, plus a small bristle brush for cleaning the dirty water tank, brush chamber, and roller.

Though it comes at a premium price, we found a lot to like about this model during testing. First, it uses what Tineco calls SmoothPower technology to help propel itself forward and back, meaning it took almost no effort to push or pull, even when the 2-liter water tank was full. And although it only came with one extra cleaning nozzle, that was both wide enough for couch cushions yet narrow enough for corners. Also, as a heated carpet cleaner with a self-wash system, we really liked how the PowerDry function sped up drying and that the automatic brush roller and suction pathway cleaning system took care of some of the post-use maintenance. The one thing we didn’t love was that it left behind a few hair clumps from our cat, even though we vacuumed first.What our tester says: “As much as I like how this model automatically adjusts to the dirt level it senses, my favorite things about it are walking over the slightly warmed carpet as the Tineco dries it and not having to do nearly as much work to clean the brush after it’s cleaned my carpets.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Tineco carpet cleaner at Amazon or Tineco.

Before we began testing, we researched more than three dozen products, ranging from small portable options to professional-style equipment and even a few steam carpet cleaners. We considered weight, cord length, and accessories, and we also looked at carpet cleaner reviews to determine what made potential picks exceptional.

We then tested 23 different carpet cleaners on a carpet swatch marked by several tough-to-clean stains, including red wine, chocolate, dirt, and oil. We also used them around the house on old stains and furniture when possible, trying all included accessories, carrying each machine up and down stairs, and monitoring how long the carpet took to dry after use. We then rated each machine on how quickly and how well it eliminated stains, overall ease of use, portability, and suction, and assigned our favorite models awards based on their strengths.

Carpet cleaning equipment often features various cleaning modes and includes several accessories. Hose and cord length affect how long the unit can continuously clean before unplugging and moving. Keeping these factors in mind when shopping can help ensure you pick the best residential carpet cleaner for your needs.

Spot-cleaning machines are lightweight, portable, and less expensive than whole-house cleaners, but their suction isn’t as strong as larger units. A handheld carpet cleaner is ideal for use on stairs, in homes with just a couple of carpeted rooms, or on area rugs. These small carpet cleaners are also good for cleaning the carpets in the car.

Whole-house or upright carpet cleaners have robust motors, powerful suction, and thick, rotating brushes that provide deep cleaning. Many models offer multiple cleaning modes and use their own cleaning solutions, making them better suited to larger homes with many carpeted rooms that see heavy traffic. A whole-house, heavy-duty carpet cleaner is ideal for lifting dirt and grime that’s settled deep into carpet or rug fibers.

Buyers will want to consider their physical limits, the amount of carpeting, and the number of levels in the home when making a decision. In general, the heavier the machine, the more powerful its suction motor and rotating brushes will be. Portable carpet cleaners, like handheld carpet cleaners, are lighter and easier to maneuver, whereas full-size upright machines capable of heavy-duty cleaning will be harder to move and store.

Cord and hose length both affect cleaning time; the less often you have to unplug and plug in, the more efficient the cleaning session. Long cords of 20 feet or more and hoses up to 10 feet are particularly helpful in large rooms and for cleaning stairs. Since some upright units don’t have hoses, buyers wanting to clean under heavy pieces of furniture will want to be careful when choosing.

Carpet-cleaner accessories are attachments that can be added to a hose or intake port for cleaning different materials, reaching difficult areas, or dealing with pet hair and odors. Some of the most common types include upholstery cleaners; crevice-cleaning attachments (handy for tight spots like the indent created where the baseboard meets the carpet); or spinning brushes that lift tough, stuck-on stains. Pet attachments include special brushes, guards, and even isolated tanks for trapping fur to prevent it from getting caught in the machine. Many machines include samples of the brand’s best carpet shampoos or cleaning solutions to help you start cleaning right away.

Before buying or renting a carpet cleaner to keep your carpet looking new, take a look at these frequently asked questions and their answers.

The price range in this lineup is $125 to $700. However, the average cost of hiring a professional carpet cleaner is about $50 per room and can be up to $600 for larger homes. This means that after just a few uses, your new carpet cleaner will have paid for itself. You also have the option of renting carpet-cleaning equipment and DIYing the job at an average price of $30 per day. Either of these routes may make sense if you have just one or two carpeted rooms, but if your entire house is carpeted or you live with small children or furry friends, it may be more cost-effective to compare carpet cleaners and invest in your own unit.

If regular vacuuming and moderate care are taken, a carpet can be cleaned once every 12 to 18 months. In an active household with pets and children, you’ll want to clean the carpet every 6 to 12 months.

The best carpet cleaner for pets can remove pet hair, odors, and stains from even the deepest fibers of the carpet. In our tests, the Shark CarpetXpert HairPro Pet With StainStriker did a great job on these tasks as well as on more serious pet messes.

Bissell recommends staying off carpet for 4 to 6 hours after cleaning, but total dry time depends on a variety of factors, including the type of carpet fibers, the pile, how much solution and water were used, room size, ventilation, humidity, and temperature. Carpet made from polyester takes between 6 and 12 hours to dry, but wool carpet takes at least 24 hours to dry. To reduce drying time, use a quick-cleaning mode, which releases less liquid, and increase ventilation by opening windows, turning on fans, and turning on heat or air conditioning.

If you want to remove surface stains or odors, shampooing your carpets will be better. To deep clean and sanitize carpet, a steam cleaner will be more effective.

How much you should spend on a carpet cleaner depends on your needs regarding features, size, and frequency of use. The carpet cleaners selected for this guide cost between $125 and $700, which reflects the typical price range for reliable models.

#7806. The Best Garage Door Thresholds of 2026, Picked by Experts

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 23, 2026 8:17 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The narrow gap at the bottom of a closed garage door is more than enough space for dirt, leaves, blowing snow, and rain to find their way inside, making a mess of your garage. Mice, rats, roaches, and other pests can also use this opening for easy access to your garage—and even to your home if you have an attached garage. However, a simple remedy for keeping out the elements and reducing the likelihood of pest infestations is a garage door threshold.

The best garage door threshold is typically made with a cushioned rubber or vinyl top and may feature an aluminum frame to install the seal to the bottom of a garage door. Based on our research, the Jin&Bao Universal Garage Door Threshold Seal Strip is our favorite for its weatherproof construction, temperature resistance, and easy installation. This guide will explore the most important factors to consider as you shop for this handy item and offer a look at some of the top products on the market to properly seal your garage.

Bottom line: Garage door thresholds are essential for protecting your garage from weather, debris, and pests, with top picks offering durability and easy installation.

The best garage door threshold can protect the flooring of a garage while keeping valuables secure and free of damage from water, debris, and pests. The top picks feature a selection of these versatile products in a variety of categories chosen with overall quality, price, and the above-mentioned considerations in mind.

For a watertight seal that lasts in any weather conditions, rely on the Jin&Bao universal garage door threshold seal strip. This option has a weatherproof construction that keeps the garage clean by preventing water, dirt, snow, dust, and leaves from coming in and withstands temperatures of -40 to 280 degrees Fahrenheit. Plus, the construction will never warp, crack, or dry out with use, so it will last in any garage threshold for years.

This option is 20 feet long by 3.7 inches wide by 0.6 inch high and is available in three colorways: green, yellow, and blue. The anti-slip ridges also keep tires in place while you’re driving over them and prevent slips and falls; the grooved base provides adhesion to the sealant on concrete, asphalt, and painted or treated garage floors. All in all, this pick is a reliable option for those who want to keep grime and dust out of their garages, making it ideal for wooded areas, garage workshops, or for those who have tractors, bikes, or trucks coming in and out.

Get the Jin&Bao garage door threshold at Amazon.

This garage door threshold from CloudBuyer measures 0.5 inches in height, 3.5 inches in width, and about 10 feet in length, though every threshold is made slightly longer to ensure the length is sufficient after customizing for the specific garage door opening. It’s easy to cut the threshold with a sharpened utility knife because it’s made with a flexible, nontoxic rubber material.

Once installed, the threshold creates a watertight seal that prevents water, snow, dust, dirt, and leaves from entering the garage. The rubber withstands extreme temperatures and won’t crack, dry out, break, or shift after installation. The garage door threshold doesn’t include the adhesive, so it will need to be purchased prior to installation.

Get the CloudBuyer garage door threshold at Amazon.

Rainwater can seep into a garage and cause damage to the tools and materials inside. Especially during winter weather, standing water in a garage may freeze and can lead to cracks in the poured concrete floor. To help prevent damage to the garage and its contents, this eco-PVC rubber garage door threshold from Weather Defender seals out water, snow, ice, and freezing winds that can drive these elements indoors. It also keeps out leaves, dust and debris, and pests like rats, mice, and snakes.

This garage door bottom seals to the floor with a grooved base, creating an ideal surface for the included adhesive. Measuring 0.63 inches in height, 3.5 inches in width, and 16.5 inches in length, it can be customized to the correct length with a utility knife. This garage door threshold also boasts an integrated yellow strip to increase nighttime visibility and anti-slip ridges for safety.

Get the Weather Defender garage door threshold at Amazon.

This universal garage door threshold from Papillon is 20 feet long, and it’s easy to customize with a utility knife for a perfect fit along the entire length of the garage door opening. The rubber threshold is 3.5 inches wide and 0.5 inches in height, preventing leaves, dirt, grass, rain, snow, snakes, and rodents from invading the garage.

The EPDM rubber is designed to withstand extreme cold and hot temperatures. The quality of the weatherproof seal doesn’t shift, crack, or dry out with temperature fluctuations, enabling it to reduce the corrosion and rust that can be caused by pooling and freezing water. The threshold also features a high-visibility yellow strip to guide drivers entering or exiting the garage in poor lighting conditions. It installs quickly with adhesive; however, the adhesive isn’t included with purchase.

Get the Papillon garage door threshold at Amazon.

This garage door threshold from ToLanbbt forms a watertight seal that keeps out dust, dirt, debris, blowing leaves, and rain. It features a grooved base that forms a tight bond between the threshold and the garage floor, making this product ideal for use on concrete, asphalt, and painted and treated surfaces. The rubber threshold also boasts anti-slip ridges and a bright yellow safety strip across the entire length to make it easier to see in dim lighting conditions.

The flexible EPDM rubber is durable and resistant to extreme high and low temperatures, so it doesn’t shift, crack, or dry out in severe conditions. The garage door threshold is 0.5 inches in height, 3.5 inches in width, and 20 feet in length and can be customized with nothing more than a utility knife. However, this product doesn’t include an adhesive.

Get the ToLanbbt garage door threshold at Amazon.

The garage is susceptible to infestations from insects, rodents, and snakes. With a garage door threshold, the gap between the garage door and the floor can be completely sealed ensuring snow, water, and frigid wind—much less a variety of critters—cannot penetrate the space. This durable vinyl garage door threshold from M-D Building Products helps insulate the garage when the door is down, slowing the transfer of heat through the door.

This garage door threshold is easy to install. The silicone adhesive is included, so it only needs to be measured, cut, and laid; no need to run out to purchase adhesive. The threshold measures 0.5 inches in height, 3.5 inches in width, and 10 feet in length, making it a good choice for a one-door garage. Additionally, the threshold can be trimmed to the length of the specific garage door opening.

Get the M-D Building Products garage door threshold kit at The Home Depot.

Garage door threshold seals look pretty similar when held up side by side, so we looked at specific features to identify the best options. Available lengths and the ability to trim the strip to size were the first critical features. We excluded thresholds made with materials that were inflexible or insufficiently waterproof.

The materials used in the best seals, from eco-PVC to natural rubber to EPDM rubber, each feature different temperature resistance and a different type of deal to garage door bottom seals. A particularly important criteria for making this list was the ability to get a good seal between the threshold and the garage flooring; extra grooves to allow glue to spread out helps, and often it’s helpful when the threshold manufacturer includes their preferred adhesive right inside the package.

Finally, while the cosmetic appearance of a garage threshold is less important than the function, visibility strips provide safety, and for some homeowners, the option of matching the threshold to the color of the existing floor is a deciding factor.

Few situations can ruin a day faster than walking to the garage in the morning to find that a late-night rainstorm has completely flooded it, ruining tools and materials in the process. To help avoid this problem, as well as issues with blowing debris and pest infestations, choose a garage door threshold that has the proper size proportions for the garage opening, watertight protection, and a soft but durable construction that will secure the garage without damaging the door through regular use. Keep reading to learn more about these and other important factors to consider when choosing the best garage door threshold.

Determine the necessary height of the garage door threshold by measuring the gap between the bottom of the garage door and the garage floor when the door is closed. To ensure that the measurements are accurate for the entire length of the gap, take measurements at semi-regular intervals.

After finding the correct height, look for a suitable garage door threshold that will fit the space while forming a tight, waterproof seal. For homes that have frequent problems with standing rainwater and storms, investing in a taller threshold is recommended. By installing this taller threshold slightly away from the garage door, it still creates a seal while allowing the door to close easily.

The required length of the garage door threshold is easy to measure. Just use a tape measure to determine the length of the garage door opening and look for a product that is slightly longer. This extra length ensures that the threshold can be customized to the specific garage door to form a watertight seal.

Typically, a garage door threshold ranges from 10 to 20 feet in length. To achieve the desired length for a specific garage, the soft rubber or vinyl can be cut with a utility knife. A threshold with an aluminum base can be customized with a hacksaw. However, instead of a single 20-foot piece of aluminum that must be cut to size, these products usually include several short aluminum strips for use as needed.

The best garage door threshold is constructed with waterproof material designed to protect the garage from dust, debris, and pests. The material is intended to be flexible for two reasons: One, so the garage door isn’t damaged when it closes, and two, so the door forms a tight seal with the garage floor to block rain, dirt and debris, and pests from entering the garage.

Common materials used to make a garage door threshold include aluminum, rubber, and vinyl. Aluminum creates a durable, stiff frame that resists shifting and can be secured to the bottom of the garage door. Rubber and vinyl are both the primary materials to make the threshold seal. These materials are waterproof, flexible, and durable, so they can withstand the weight of the garage door while keeping out water, dirt, and pests.

The purpose of a garage door threshold is to protect the garage itself and all the tools, appliances, vehicles, and other valuables contained inside. This generally refers to keeping rainwater, standing water, or melting snow from running into the garage and flooding the floor, but protection doesn’t stop there.

The best garage door threshold can also act as a physical barrier that prevents leaves, dirt, and other debris from being blown into the garage. Additionally, the seal can keep out pests, like mice, rats, snakes, and roaches, while helping to insulate the garage from outdoor temperatures. This simple device secures the garage, creating a more pleasant place to store items and work on projects.

Keep in mind that many products do not include adhesive, so this may need to be a separate purchase before installing the garage door threshold.

For more information about how these garage door seals work and how to install them, read below to find the answers to some of the most frequently asked questions about garage door thresholds.

Garage door seals are typically made of vinyl or rubber, which are resistant to water. The threshold is installed on the floor of the garage, so the door closes on the threshold. This creates a seal when the garage door is fully closed that protects the garage from water, dust, and pests.

Garage door strip replacement isn’t difficult. Just clean the area, mark the space where you plan to install the threshold, apply adhesive, and place the threshold. Close the garage door after installation and allow the adhesive to cure for 24 hours before opening it.

Door thresholds are normally installed with the use of an adhesive, regardless of the type of garage floor. As long as the concrete floor is clean and relatively level, it’s easy and safe to install a garage door threshold on a concrete floor with adhesive.
